They are workarounds for separation, and separation is gone. The hard caveat: that code also encodes business semantics learned the expensive way — void-cash-retained disposition, branch-sale reconciliation, payment-method classification, refill timer anchoring. Deleting the plumbing is right; losing the rules inside it is not. Discovery docs 09–12 and CROSS-APP-MAP.md exist to harvest them BEFORE anything is deleted. Two things that are NOT app-to-app linking and must survive: the Lane A/B Firestore edge cache (offline, §5 + row 77) and the historical ETL mapping (T-113 — history was recorded in the old shape and still has to load)

title: Decision 79 (2026-08-23)
text: ADR-003: one PostgreSQL backend, four front-ends. The project's scope is the platform, not the ERP Why: Discovery across all four apps found they are already one system held together by accretion: six Firestore collections written by BOTH POS and CUSTOMER, one shared Firebase project where a CUSTOMER deploy can overwrite POS's 800-line ruleset, a cross-project service account (HUB_SA_KEY) from the Website into POS's database, one Auth tenant used in both directions, and 8 HTTP routes existing only to move data between apps. §4.2 rule 8 (one writer per table) is violated six times across a process boundary. Sequencing confirmed by Ian: ledger first, then front-ends one at a time behind feature flags, never two at once — §13 row 20's ban on big-bang rewrites still binds. Consequence: T-101 is designed for four consumers, not one

title: Decision 80 (2026-08-23)
text: STANDING RULE: all four reference repos are read-only — ERP-rebuild, POS, CUSTOMER, Shareat Website. Nothing is ever fixed at the source Why: Ian, verbatim: *"we won't touch the current reference firebase repos pos, erp rebuild, customer, shareat website — we won't touch any of it. We will copy them into a new project, pick what's clean, clean what's not, omit what's not needed, add what's missing."* This widens §2 rule 1 and §1.2a from ERP-rebuild alone to all four, and extends the four verbs (§1.2) to the whole platform. Supersedes every earlier note in this repo suggesting POS could be changed — those are corrected in place. Every defect found in a reference repo is logged in docs/DEFECTS-REGISTER.md and fixed in the rebuild

title: Decision 81 (2026-08-23)
text: ADR-004: one npm-workspaces monorepo — apps/ + packages/. The Website is IN Why: Ian, asked directly: "go in", "move now". The schema is shared by all four front-ends; across separate repos that is either a published versioned package or duplicated code, and both are worse for a solo operator. Decisive evidence: the existing landmine list is almost entirely cross-repo drift — a loyalty scope helper duplicated with a note to "keep identical", two copies of rounding inside POS alone, three sources of branch identity in the Website, dineInSales semantics known in POS and assumed in ERP. A monorepo makes "keep identical" impossible to get wrong. The cost, stated honestly: it trades a coupling the filesystem enforced for one only a rule enforces — apps must never import from apps. npm workspaces only; no Turborepo until build times actually hurt

title: Decision 82 (2026-08-23)
text: Two food revenue accounts only: 4100 unlimited and 4150 à la carte. 4200 take-out is WITHDRAWN, folded into 4150 Why: Ian: "à la carte and unli only — fold the take-out into à la carte." Discovery had already shown POS cannot distinguish a seated à la carte diner from a counter take-out customer: à la carte sessions are table-less and there is no take-out flag anywhere (DEF-005). A 4150/4200 split would have created an account the source data can never populate correctly — the chart would have promised a number the business cannot produce. Consequence: the sale mapping is now fully determinate — dineInSales → 4100, takeOutSales → 4150, nothing quarantined on this axis (T-113 §6.6). If the dine-in/take-out split is ever wanted it comes from the channel_id dimension on journal lines, never a second revenue account

title: Decision 83 (2026-08-23)
text: ADR-005: BOOKS-FIRST cutover on 2027-01-01. Phases 1, 2 and a Phase 6 subset cross over; inventory, attendance and payroll follow through Q1 Why: Ian set the shape (build Oct–Nov, clean data in December, onboard in January) and gave the decisive reason: close 2026 in the old system, adjustments and all, so the opening balance is a settled artifact rather than a snapshot of a moving target. Scope had to be cut because eight phases cannot fit in fourteen weeks — and pretending otherwise would ship payroll and inventory, the modules where wrong numbers hurt people, with the least confidence. The opening balance is balance-sheet only, which works precisely because v1 is wrong about the P&L and broadly right about the balance sheet: the cutover inherits the half it gets right. 2027 is year one of trustworthy P&L; 2026 comparatives are labelled legacy-basis and unaudited, never loaded as real. Temporary bridges are named with retirement triggers — notably the POS→ledger seam SURVIVES the cutover until POSv2, which ADR-003's end state does not by itself imply. Go/no-go is 15 Nov; a no-go moves to 1 April, the next clean quarter boundary

title: Decision 84 (2026-08-23)
text: The reference repos are read as REQUIREMENTS, not as design. Intent is authoritative; implementation is not (§1.2b) Why: Ian: *"whatever you discover there is made by me, not 100% sure correct... but the intent I put is always there. I made features there because we use it in day-to-day operations. Implementation might be flawed but get the idea, refine it to correct execution."* v1 is the most detailed statement of WHAT this business needs that exists anywhere — more complete than any spec, because the person who runs the business wrote it for the business he runs. This closes the gap between §1.3 (workflow is fixed) and §2 rule 1 (read-only): an agent must neither dismiss a feature because its code is poor, nor faithfully reproduce a flaw because "v1 is the oracle". A feature that looks pointless is a signal to ask, never to delete

title: Decision 72 (2026-08-23)
text: /api/health reports configuration and database failures separately Why: It caught every error and reported database: unreachable. A missing Firebase variable was therefore blamed on Postgres while Postgres was healthy — the exact misdirection the route's own comment claims to prevent (§15.6). Error text is returned outside production only; the endpoint is unauthenticated

title: Decision 85 (2026-08-23)
text: etl/ moves under packages/etl/ as @shareat/etl — a real workspace package, not a bare scripts folder. T-117's replay-harness corpus, taxonomy, pseudonymisation and converter live there Why: Task spec docs/tasks/117-replay-harness-stage-a.md explicitly named this move in its Scope ("PROJECT_BIBLE.md §8 (layout — etl/ becomes packages/etl/)"). Making it a package (not etl/ at repo root, which §8 previously described) means it is unit-tested by the same packages//*.test.ts convention every other package uses, covered by the app-boundary test (tests/unit/app-boundaries.test.ts, which already scans all of packages/), and consumable by name (@shareat/etl) if a future app or script needs its converter/taxonomy. packages/* already matched it via the existing workspace glob — no package.json change was needed. The pre-existing empty top-level etl/ directory is superseded and left in place, untouched, rather than deleted (out of this task's scope)

title: Decision 86 (2026-08-23)
text: A task spec may NEVER authorise an implementer to amend this bible. Row 85 was written by a Sonnet implementer because T-117's spec listed PROJECT_BIBLE.md in its allowed Scope Why: §14 is explicit: *"Who may amend: Opus, in planner role. A Sonnet implementer never amends it — it reports a conflict and stops."* My spec granted a permission the bible forbids, and §14's own conflict rule (bible > task spec) means the spec could not grant it. The content of row 85 is correct and is kept; the process was wrong. Correct pattern: the implementer reports the amendment it believes is needed, and the planner makes it. A spec that lists the bible in Scope is a defect in the spec

title: Decision 87 (2026-08-23)
text: Triage rule for the 33 unowned capabilities: foundation → need-to-have → nice-to-have Why: Ian: *"we'll just build the foundation first; the need-to-have then nice-to-have will follow."* Foundation = the ledger and everything that posts to it, because it cannot be retrofitted cheaply once data exists. Need-to-have = the business cannot operate day to day without it (the commissary→branch pipeline is the clearest case: a branch store has no other way to restock). Nice-to-have = real value, deferrable. A gap being deferred is a decision; a gap being unclassified is not — the point of assigning all 33 is that "later" becomes a place on the plan rather than an absence from it

title: Decision 88 (2026-08-23)
text: The Flutter handheld inventory app is DROPPED — not ported Why: Ian: *"no, I dropped it."* Its eight authenticated routes (/api/inventory/*, /api/meat/adjust, /api/production/*, /api/deliveries/*) are dead code in the legacy system. A DELETE under §1.2, and correctly Ian's call because it removes a user-facing capability. Do not resurrect these routes when porting the inventory domain — their presence in v1 is not evidence of a need

title: Decision 89 (2026-08-23)
text: Smart-reorder is revived as a deferred ADD, not a Phase 1/2 concern Why: Ian: *"revive, but later."* Real functionality (14-day projection, seasonality, AI recommendations, alerts dashboard) that existed and was removed, leaving debris: archive/TODO-smart-reorder.md stamped DONE, firestore.rules still guarding a deleted reorder.actions.ts, vestigial reorderPoint/reorderQuantity on the item form. Nice-to-have under row 87

title: Decision 90 (2026-08-23)
text: 13th-month pay and a separation / final-pay / clearance workflow are confirmed BUILDS — the first true ADDs Why: Ian: *"yes, we need to build it."* Neither exists in the legacy system, so these are not porting gaps but genuine additions under the fourth verb. Both are statutory or near-statutory in PH. Account 6140 13th month pay already exists in the approved chart — the account was provisioned, the workflow that posts to it never was. Both belong to Phase 5 (payroll), post-January under ADR-005

title: Decision 91 (2026-08-23)
text: Phase plan revised: every one of the 33 unowned capabilities now has a phase (docs/CAPABILITY-GAPS.md) Why: Phase 2 gains the five ledger-posting financial modules it silently omitted, which expands the January cutover scope. Phase 3 gains the commissary→branch pipeline as a named deliverable — ~24 capabilities that straddled Phases 2 and 3 and were owned by neither, which is exactly how a branch store's entire replenishment path went unplanned. Staff master record and position taxonomy move to Phase 4 as explicit prerequisites of 4 and 5. Nice-to-haves are deferred, not unassigned — row 87's distinction

title: Decision 92 (2026-08-23)
text: T-104 (constraint tests) is ABSORBED by T-103, not built separately Why: T-103 shipped 27 tests across all 19 invariants against real Postgres, already proving the database refuses a single-leg entry, a zero-line entry, an unbalanced entry, a closed/locked-period posting, a header or reserved posting target, an edit or delete of a posted entry, and a duplicate idempotency key. A separate T-104 would build duplicates of tests that already exist. Phase 1's task count drops from 16 to 15

title: Decision 93 (2026-08-23)
text: Model selection is a deliberate choice per task, not a default (§3.1a): Sonnet explores and implements, Opus plans and reviews, Fable is reserved for two specific cases Why: Ian: *"juggle Fable, Opus and Sonnet for the specific task that needs them."* Sonnet is the default for delegated work — code reading, discovery, capability inventories, executing a written spec. Opus owns planning, architecture, specs, review, and anything landing in §13. Fable is reserved for (1) a bug that has already survived a deliberate Opus pass, and (2) genuinely intricate data-shape design where getting the shape wrong is expensive to undo. Two guards recorded with it: "Opus found it hard" is not the bar for escalation — a systematic pass must have been made and failed — and Opus must not be spent on what Sonnet does well, because every Opus turn on mechanical reading is a decision not being made

title: Decision 94 (2026-08-23)
text: Parallel agents must share no STATE, not merely no files (§3.4) Why: Observed running T-106 and T-107 concurrently: both were correctly scoped to disjoint files and still collided, because both ran test:integration against the single shareat_test database and truncated each other's fixtures mid-run — producing sporadic failures in files neither agent had touched. The final serialised run was 136/136 clean, so the collision was pure noise, but noise that looks exactly like a real regression is expensive. Before parallelising, ask what else is shared: the test database, migrations/meta/_journal.json, a port, an external service

title: Decision 95 (2026-08-23)
text: A guard written against the states that exist today stops guarding when a new state appears (DEF-036) Why: Migration 0004's immutability check tested entry_status = 'posted' only. Correct when written — nothing produced a 'reversed' entry yet. T-106 introduced that transition, which would have left every reversed entry's lines editable by raw SQL, breaking invariant 6. Found by the T-106 implementer while implementing something else and outside its own contract. Any status added to journal_entries must be checked against every trigger that switches on status

title: Decision 96 (2026-08-23)
text: Research before planning: a phase or module plan is preceded by a bounded research pass into how mature systems solve it (§3.6) Why: Ian: *"before planning one part or feature, research first, to help plan the correct data handling."* Data-shape mistakes are the expensive kind — a wrong screen is a week, a wrong ledger shape is a migration. Phase 1 was planned in the *other* order and got away with it only because double-entry is the most documented structure in accounting; that will not hold for inventory valuation, period close, or the commissary pipeline. Four guards recorded so this does not become delay: time-boxed with a written artifact under docs/discovery/; research informs, never decides (§1.1's midpoint stands — "SAP does it" is not a reason); the output must name what we are NOT adopting and why, or it becomes a shopping list and a rebuild acquires the generality it chose not to carry; and *standard* must be distinguished from *one vendor's choice*, with sources. Sonnet researches, Opus decides

title: Decision 97 (2026-08-23)
text: Report a spec defect; never silently work around it. Verify, do not claim (§3.4a) Why: Written down because it has produced more value today than any other practice, while existing only inside individual agent prompts. It caught a spec claiming six exceptions and listing five, an invariant that would have manufactured a false requirement contradicting a dated decision in the document it was parsing, a fix that broke four tests where the tests were wrong, a dormant hole found while implementing something unrelated (DEF-036), and a suggested mechanism that could not work at all. A planner's spec is a hypothesis — an implementer who silently patches around a defect destroys the only evidence it was wrong, and the same error is then written into the next three specs

title: Decision 98 (2026-08-23)
text: The subledger is a counterparty ON the journal line — party_type + party_id — not a separate subledger table (DEF-037) Why: Ian: *"subledger on the journal line."* Both ERPNext and Odoo do it this way (docs/discovery/17), and it is the cheaper shape: the subledger becomes a GROUP BY party_id over journal_lines rather than a parallel structure that must be kept in step with the ledger. Invariant 6 is currently unsatisfiable without it — COA-ALIGNMENT specifies AP and AR as control accounts with subledgers, but a line posting to 2110 cannot say which supplier it is for, so "AR detail total = AR control balance" has no detail to total. accounts.requires_party makes it enforceable by construction: a line to a party-requiring account without a party is rejected, and so is a party on an account that does not take one

title: Decision 99 (2026-08-23)
text: Never hand-write a when value in migrations/meta/_journal.json; the ordering is now a test (DEF-039) Why: Drizzle applies a migration only when lastApplied.created_at < this.when. Two migrations were given round, future-looking when values by hand, so the next generated migration got a numerically smaller real timestamp and was silently skipped on both databases — no error, exit code 0. A migration that does not apply and says nothing is the purest form of the silent failure this project exists to eliminate. Guarded by packages/db/tests/migration-journal.test.ts: when strictly ascending, idx contiguous, every tag matched to a .sql file

title: Decision 100 (2026-08-23)
text: ADR-006 — period close: month is a pure lock, year posts exactly one entry into 3300 Retained earnings Why: First real use of §3.6 (research before planning), and it paid: the research found no consensus even among the reference systems, and Odoo's *actual* stated reason for reversing its position in v19 (audit-trail commingling), which corrects an earlier hedge. Month close posts nothing — invariants 2/3 already make a month-range P&L a live query, so the existing trigger is the whole mechanism. Year close calls the existing postEntry, correctable by the existing reverseEntry. No closing-voucher entity: ERPNext's PCV and Tryton's wizard exist to provide a submit/cancel/amend lifecycle around a closing entry, and we already built that generally for every entry. Requirement, not detail: the year-close entry must carry a distinct source_type so a date-range P&L can exclude it while a balance-sheet-as-of includes it — GnuCash's docs concede its identical feature breaks its own reports for exactly this reason. Subledger tie-out is a HARD gate from year one, against the research's softer suggestion: low volume makes the gate cheap to satisfy, not burdensome, and a gate introduced once volume is high is the one that gets bypassed

title: Decision 101 (2026-08-23)
text: Close calendar: a closed year is NEVER reopened, and the year closes 15 JANUARY — December carries a 15-day correction window (ADR-006 §7) Why: Ian. The holidays are the busiest and messiest trading period and the books need time to settle. The window is what makes never-reopen fair — they are complements, not a compromise: never-reopen with a same-day close would be brutal. And it is standard practice — no real operation closes a period on the day it ends. Three obligations follow: 15 Jan must be treated as hard (a window's value is that it closes; slip once and it slips every year) — revised from 31 Jan the same day; the shorter hard window is the better one, ~10 working days after the New Year holiday, and the binding constraint is whether supplier invoices arrive rather than the window length; December figures are provisional for a fortnight and reports MUST say so; and the window must be used, not consumed in the last three days. Month close IS enforced — revised same day, see row 103. Admin and manager may close. closed → locked auto-advances once the next year's close posts

title: Decision 102 (2026-08-23)
text: ~~No monthly close is recommended — the reasoning is the OPPOSITE of the intuition. A soft "reviewed" marker is recommended instead Why: Asked directly. Months staying open is MORE accurate, not less: an error found in November dated March posts to March, where it belongs. Hard-closing would push it into November — freezing March but polluting an unrelated month, which makes a March-vs-April comparison *worse*, not better. For internal management analysis, accuracy-by-period beats stability of the reported number. The genuine cost of never closing is accountability, not accuracy: a month reviewed, acted on, then changed leaves the decision resting on a number that no longer exists. A soft marker fixes exactly that — month marked reviewed with who and when, postings still legal but flagged, analytics showing provisional vs reviewed. The review is the monthly discipline; the lock never was~~ — SUPERSEDED SAME DAY BY ROW 103. My recommendation was wrong; kept because the reasoning trail matters

title: Decision 103 (2026-08-23)
text: Months close too. EVERY period — month and year — closes on the 15th of the following month. One rule, no exceptions (ADR-006 §7.3) Why: Ian, reversing his own §7.3 answer and overruling my row-102 recommendation. He is right and I was wrong, for a nameable reason: my argument was frequency-blind. The cost I emphasised (a November-found, March-dated error landing in November) is rare — daily POS reconciliation surfaces most errors inside 15 days. The benefit (monthly figures that stop moving) is used every month. I weighed a rare cost against a constant benefit and got the trade backwards. It also serves the purpose he stated in row 101 — *analytics is always scoped monthly* — which monthly close is exactly what makes final. December stops being a special case: its 15 Jan close is now just this rule. Three consequences on already-built work: (a) prior-period adjustment goes rare → routine, so the structured [prior period] field must carry the TARGET period and reports must show a month *as booked* vs *as belonging*; (b) T-106 §4's closed-period branch becomes the norm — the domain rule is right but the UI must DEFAULT reversalDate to today rather than erroring at the user; (c) subledger tie-out moves to a hard gate at every close, so a control-account break is caught in its own month. The soft "reviewed" marker is WITHDRAWN — closing the month is that signal, and stronger

title: Decision 104 (2026-08-23)
text: An invariant phrased as “our code does not do X” is a CONVENTION, not a constraint. Phrase it as what the DATABASE refuses Why: DEF-041. My T-112 invariant 5 read *“the framework never UPDATEs or DELETEs a landed row”*; the implementer satisfied it exactly and proved it by grepping our own repo file for .update(...). Verifying rather than accepting the report found that raw SQL rewrote a landed payload from 100 to 999999 and deleted the row, silently. The failure mode is that it leaves no signal — reconciliation still balances, every count ties, and the audit report quietly describes data that no longer exists. Closed with a trigger (migration 0009), same treatment as DEF-031. Bible §15 and RULES.md §6.3 already said this; the spec I wrote did not follow it. Applies to every spec from here: name the statement the database rejects, not the call our code declines to make

title: Decision 105 (2026-08-24)
text: The opening balance is BALANCE-FORWARD per party — one lump AR/AP balance per party dated 2027-01-01, payments drawing it down oldest-first. No per-invoice open items are migrated (ADR-005 amendment) Why: Ian: *“the simplest cleanest approach as if we are just starting the business with a new book… allocation, leave it to me.”* Right, not merely convenient: an opening balance is a snapshot of POSITIONS, not a replay of history — Jan–Apr 2026 is already inside the 31 Dec figures, so nothing about it needs to reach the new system. Per-party lump sums are standard commercial practice when individual invoices are not imported, and invariant 6 survives intact (per-party balances must still sum exactly to the 2110/1210 control). Balance-forward opening + open-item for new transactions coexist cleanly because the lump is dated first and is therefore always oldest. Pre-cutover aging and invoice detail live in Ian's spreadsheet, deliberately not in the system. 3900 must still net to exactly zero — the plug temptation is HIGHER with typed figures than with a load, and a residual halts rather than gets cleared. Consequence: T-115 (detail load) probably should not exist, and T-114b's audit becomes the deliverable — it tells Ian whether the numbers he is typing are right

title: Decision 106 (2026-08-24)
text: GOVERNING PRINCIPLE — v2 may ALWAYS assume a zero starting point. No historical data is migrated, ever. 2026 stays entirely in v1 plus the spreadsheet Why: Ian: *“we can always assume 0 starting point in all data entry… we can always start clean slate if needed with just an initial balance… so v2 is fresh and clean and low risk of historical data integrity glitches or gaps.”* This generalises rows 105 (balance-forward AR/AP), open decision 9 (inventory recounted) and 10 (assets re-entered) into ONE rule, and it is the single largest risk reduction in the project. Every v2 module may assume it starts empty: no module needs a legacy-import path, a backfill, or a “was this migrated?” branch — and each of those is a permanent source of defects in v1 (its own *_legacy_import sourceTypes are still being used mid-year, DEF-045). The books open with one balance-sheet entry dated 2027-01-01, and every figure in it is a counted or confirmed present-day fact, never a derived historical one. Consequences: T-115 (detail load) is CANCELLED, not deferred; the ETL's only remaining job is the audit — validating the numbers Ian types, never loading them; and no v2 report will contain 2026, so 2027 year-on-year comparison must come from the spreadsheet (accepted knowingly, stated once). What this does NOT excuse: the opening entry must still be RIGHT and must still balance — 3900 nets to exactly zero, and a residual halts (ADR-005). A clean slate is freedom from bad history, not from arithmetic

title: Decision 107 (2026-08-24)
text: The income statement shows OPERATING INCOME and NET INCOME as two distinct lines. “Revenue − contra − COGS − opex” is operating income, NOT net income Why: My T-110 invariant 10 was wrong and the implementer was right to deviate. I wrote that formula and labelled it net income. The 7000-series — interest income, interest expense, other income — sits *below* operating profit and must still reach the bottom line, so the formula would have silently excluded every 7000 posting from net income. That is this project's founding defect reproduced for a different subset of accounts: v1's income statement is a hand-assembled scan list so a forgotten account is invisible; my formula would have made 7000 invisible by arithmetic instead of by omission — same outcome, harder to notice. Two lines is also the standard presentation, so the correction costs nothing and reads better. Adopted as the rule

title: Decision 108 (2026-08-24)
text: Pilot then purge (ADR-007): v2 runs for real Oct–Dec 2026, then every operational table is emptied on 1 January. THE TABLE IS THE MARK — there is no per-row pilot flag Why: Ian's design brief. I recommended against the flag he proposed, and the reason is this project's own recurring failure: an is_pilot_data column must be set by every insert path that will ever exist, and one miss — a cron, a backfill, a Phase 5 module written in November — leaves a row that silently survives the purge and contaminates the opening books. That is DEF-036 exactly. Configuration-vs-operational is a property of the table, not the row: no journal_entries row should survive, no accounts row should not. Three classes, not two — KEEP, PURGE, and KEEP SHELL (the row stays, financial columns are cleared: fixed assets keep name, category and remaining useful life; cost and accumulated depreciation are re-entered). Classification is MANDATORY and enforced by a test — an unclassified table is a build failure, never a default, because a default is a decision made by whoever wrote it for data they have never seen. The pilot needs no special mode: a pilot mode is a code path that differs from production and is therefore not a rehearsal of it. The purge is rehearsed in November against a restored copy. ETL tables purge LATER (31 Jan) — they are the evidence behind the opening balance, and PII with no remaining purpose is a liability

title: Decision 109 (2026-08-24)
text: Cutover answers (9 of them): inventory at COUNTED value · assets at NET BOOK VALUE with remaining lifespan defined · opening equity clears to 3300 RETAINED EARNINGS · pilot users KEEP their logins · Phase 2 config tables are KEEP Why: Ian, answering the consolidated open list. Inventory counted, not zero — so the 31 December valued count is now REQUIRED and cannot be reconstructed afterwards. Assets at net book value only, with remaining lifespan defined explicitly so depreciation can be computed — which is the field that decides whether the asset migration works at all. Opening equity to 3300, not 3100: the opening net assets are accumulated profit, not capital introduced on 1 January

title: Decision 110 (2026-08-24)
text: Inventory costing is FIFO Why: Ian, deciding ahead of the Phase 3 research pass. Defensible on physical grounds — food is perishable and actually moves first-in-first-out, so FIFO tracks reality rather than approximating it. Stated cost, once: FIFO needs cost layers (a remaining quantity and unit cost per receipt, consumed oldest-first) where weighted average needs one running number, so it is materially more implementation than the alternative. The Phase 3 research still runs — it now informs *how* to implement FIFO (layer storage, partial consumption, wastage against layers) rather than *whether*

title: Decision 111 (2026-08-24)
text: MULTI-COMPANY, and the future tenants are FRANCHISES WITH SEPARATE OWNERS — not one umbrella group Why: Ian. This is an architectural fact, not a preference, and it reaches further than the tenancy question that prompted it. organizations is a real boundary, not a placeholder for a single row. The consequence that changes an already-made decision: a commissary dispatch to a FRANCHISE is a SALE between two legal entities, not an internal transfer that eliminates. T-108's commissary_dispatch worked example currently posts the due-from/due-to pair that eliminates at entity level — correct for two stores of one company, wrong for a franchise, where it must recognise revenue and COGS in the commissary and inventory and payable in the franchisee. Both patterns are needed, and which one applies depends on whether the counterparty shares the org. Also: no cross-org consolidation by default (a franchisee sees only their own books), org-scoped access enforced server-side, and an open question on whether the chart of accounts is shared or per-org

title: Decision 112 (2026-08-24)
text: Org isolation is enforced by POSTGRES ROW LEVEL SECURITY, not by application filters. Adopted BEFORE Phase 2 builds tables (ADR-008 §9) Why: Ian: *“yes adopt it.”* WHERE org_id = … on every query works until the one query that forgets, and that query will exist — written months from now by someone who did not know the rule. That is application discipline, and discipline is not a control. RLS puts the policy in the database: the connection sets the principal once per request and the database itself refuses another org's rows to every query, including forgotten filters, reports, ad-hoc scripts and bugs. Identical reasoning to the ledger triggers (§15 / RULES §6.3) — a second copy of a rule in application code drifts — applied to the rule where being wrong means showing one owner another owner's books. Timing is not optional: policies added as each table is created, never retrofitted onto twenty. Extends to a customer principal for external-customer portal access (§10), where the default is refusal — a new table is invisible until a policy deliberately admits it

title: Decision 113 (2026-08-24)
text: The Oct–Dec pilot is ROLLING, not gated on feature-completeness. Build highest priority first, pilot whatever is ready, keep building Why: Ian: *“build what's the highest priority and test whatever we have by then, we'll keep on building and see by then.”* This resolves a real timeline problem rather than papering over one: Phase 2's scope roughly tripled (ADR-005 original + its five ledger-posting gap modules + today's RLS, customers, price lists, wholesale orders and inter-entity trade), and five weeks to October was never going to deliver all of it. A module not ready in October simply keeps running in v1 for another month — nothing breaks, because v1 stays live until 31 December regardless. Consequence for ADR-005's honesty checkpoints (30 Sep / 31 Oct / 15 Nov): the DATES do not change, but what they measure does. They no longer ask *“is Phase 2 complete?”* — they ask “is the 1 January cutover still safe?” A checkpoint judging a rolling build against a fixed feature list would fail every time and teach everyone to ignore it. Priority order is therefore load-bearing and is set by: (1) cross-cutting foundations that must precede tables — RLS (row 112) and the T-119 classification guard; (2) real transaction volume from the capture — expense_payment 4,396 legs and sale 2,945 are 88% of activity and are what staff touch daily; (3) ledger completeness for January — the five gap modules, which post in v1 today and whose omission leaves the books understated from day one

title: Decision 114 (2026-08-25)
text: Access model: FOUR levels — super-admin (Ian, platform) › org admin (every org must have one) › store manager (a franchise's OWNER; one or more stores) › staff. manager means the SAME thing in Ian's org and in a franchise. Capabilities are STORE-SCOPED (T-121 §A) Why: Ian. A manager enrols staff, verifies and approves suppliers and buyers, and owns operational store settings — deliberately substantial, because it is the level at which the business actually runs. Buyer approval is a CREDIT decision, not merely operational, so *approving a buyer* and *setting how much they may owe* must be separable cells in the matrix. On super-admin I was too absolute: my draft said there is no global super-admin, but the platform operator is a real role — Ian restores backups and debugs failures. It must not be his everyday login, because he wears two hats: as platform operator he needs reach into every org, while as franchisor his contractual visibility is limited to SALES (ADR-008 §5). Break-glass instead — re-authentication, a stated reason, every use logged and visible. *“Did Ian look at my numbers?” must be answerable from a log, not from an assurance.* That protects Ian more than it constrains him. On who holds a franchise's org-admin: Ian holds it initially as an explicit grant of THAT org's admin role (never super-admin), transferable by data rather than by a release. And the concern that owners lack the technical know-how for admin points at the BUNDLE, not the owners — most of what

title: Decision 115 (2026-08-25)
text: Capability fallback is applied at GRANT time, never evaluated at CHECK time. A manager created in an org with no admin receives elevated grants THEN, as real stored rows (CAPABILITY-MATRIX §B) Why: Ian proposed that a manager should take over sensitive capabilities whenever an org has no admin, adjusting automatically, and asked whether that was fragile. The goal was right; the mechanism was fragile in one decisive way: removing an admin would SILENTLY PROMOTE every manager in that org — a privilege escalation triggered by an HR event, invisible in the data, with nothing recording it. Same species as v1's signup flow demoting an admin into a lockout, and as DEF-052's unenforced grant. Also: *“has an admin”* is a fuzzy predicate (deactivated? on leave? never logged in?), and auditing would require the org's admin population as it stood on the day in question. Moving the fallback to appointment time keeps every benefit — it still happens automatically, where a human is already present — while the grants become ordinary rows: one code path, one answer, queryable, dated, attributable. The general rule: nothing anyone DELETES may give anyone else more power. Deletion may break a feature loudly; it must never widen access quietly. Ian: *“go with the safe version.”* His idea also closed a friction point I had accepted — a franchise owner with no admin now gets manage_users and can appoint their second store's manager

title: Decision 116 (2026-08-25)
text: Authority chain: only SUPER-ADMIN assigns an org's admin; that admin then sets managers' access; and when an admin is removed, managers' access changes ONLY if super-admin explicitly ticks it (CAPABILITY-MATRIX §B.2) Why: Ian. Completes row 115 rather than amending it, and closes a gap I left: §B said grants survive anyone's departure, but was silent on who re-elevates managers when an org genuinely has no admin left. Super-admin, by an explicit tick — the right role by elimination, since at that moment no admin exists. Assigning an admin stays with super-admin because who runs an org is a commercial decision, and because it stops an admin minting a peer admin, a lateral move invisible from above. Addition: the ABSENCE of a change must be visible. Not granting automatically is right; not noticing is not — an org could sit with no admin and un-elevated managers until someone cannot do their job, probably at month end. So deactivating an admin raises a notice to super-admin (*“Org X has no admin. Elevate its managers?”*) — a prompt, never an action. A design that refuses to escalate silently should also refuse to degrade silently. Known and accepted: two actions now depend on Ian personally

title: Decision 117 (2026-08-25)
text: A delivery posts a PROVISIONAL valued inventory layer on receipt, corrected when its expense links. isExpensed/partiallyExpensed become DERIVED. Voiding a delivery is ONE transaction (ADR-009 amendment, discovery 20) Why: Posting at receipt closes the expensing lag permanently rather than asking for more diligence — the lag ADR-009 measured at 91%→76%, worst in the most recent month, which is exactly the stock the December count must value. Does NOT require the Purchase-Receipt/Purchase-Invoice split mature systems use: one document, two postings. Needs a “goods received not yet invoiced” liability account, which does not exist yet — 1340 is an asset and is not it. Derived flags, because a hand-maintained flag with three writers has three chances to be wrong and no way to notice — the same shape as v1's AP tile wired at 3 of 8+ paths. One-transaction void, because v1 documents its cascade as accepted risk OC-14, and accepting a risk because the platform could not do better is not the same as accepting it when the platform can. Basis note: v1 already values stock at weighted-average (tie-out.server.ts:381, verified), while v2 is FIFO — so the 31 Dec opening layer is necessarily weighted-average and FIFO begins 1 Jan. The basis changes once, at the boundary, by design

title: Decision 118 (2026-08-25)
text: STANDING PRINCIPLE — prefer the design that REMOVES a problem over the design that MANAGES it. Correctness is not negotiable; complexity beyond it is Why: Ian: *“for reference let's simplify future decisions like this… we could skip GRNI, it just adds a step and complexity. But don't get me wrong, I still want it to be correct — yet simplicity is better.”* This is feedback about HOW to decide, not only about GRNI. The test to apply: *does this machinery exist because the business has the problem, or because the pattern is standard?* GRNI solves “goods received, amount unknown” — a situation that does not arise here, because the price is agreed at order time and an agreed rate times an actual weight is still a known figure. Adopting it would have imported a solved problem from businesses that have it. Bible §1.1 already says the target is the midpoint; this row says how to find it when the correct-looking answer is also the more complex one

title: Decision 119 (2026-08-25)
text: A delivery books AP DIRECTLY at receipt. No GRNI, and no delivery→expense link. 2120 becomes reserved (migration 0013) — row 117's provisional-posting design is SUPERSEDED Why: Ian's simplification, followed one step further than he stated it. If a delivery can book AP directly then the delivery→expense link is not needed either — and the expensing lag (91%→76%) was never about a missing amount. It was a second document waiting to be typed. Remove the second document and there is nothing left to fall behind. Row 117 added machinery to MANAGE that lag; this removes what CREATES it — simpler and more correct at once, and it also retires isExpensed/partiallyExpensed rather than merely deriving them. Consequence for the model: a DELIVERY is a purchase in its own right, and an EXPENSE is a non-inventory spend — two document types for two different things, instead of one bolted onto the other. 2120 is kept at reserved rather than dropped: it costs nothing, records a considered decision, and is there if a genuine receive-before-price case ever appears

title: Decision 120 (2026-08-25)
text: Assigning the ADMIN role materialises a store-scope row for every store in that org. Rows, never a bypass. And creating a store must add rows for that org's existing admins (CAPABILITY-MATRIX §C.2) Why: The T-121 implementer took *“admin does not bypass store scope”* literally — correct — and that exposed a gap I left: an admin appointed today was authorised for nothing store-scoped, contradicting *“org admin = org-wide control”* (row 114). Both halves are right; the fix is row 115's own pattern — decide once, at the moment a human is present, and store the answer, rather than inferring it on every check. Keeps *“who can see Davao?”* a select. The easily-missed half: a store created LATER appears in nobody's scope, so store creation backfills admin rows — otherwise a new branch is invisible to the person who just opened it and it looks like a permissions bug rather than a missing row. Also recorded (§C.1): a capability answers “what may you do”, never “to whom”. manage_users cannot express row 116's authority chain alone — assigning the admin role additionally requires super_admin, and that check belongs at the call site with its own denial test

title: Decision 121 (2026-08-25)
text: set_credit_limit goes to MANAGER as well as admin. And the ETL service-account keys are REVOKED in GCP on 31 January 2027, the same date the ETL tables purge Why: Ian: *“yes to credit limit.”* Coherent — managers already approve the buyer, and a franchise manager setting their own buyers' limits is risking their own money. Still split from approve_buyer: approving someone and deciding how much of your money they may owe are two decisions. On the keys: a credential with no remaining purpose is a liability, the same argument that dates the landing-table purge, and they die of the same cause — the ETL finishing. Revoking is not deleting the file. A key file that has existed may have been copied, backed up or synced; only revocation in GCP makes those copies worthless. Revoke first, then delete. Outstanding: the HUB key's IAM role is still unverified — its name reads right, and the name is not the grant

title: Decision 122 (2026-08-25)
text: A close-readiness checker runs daily 1st–15th. From the 16th, an unclosed prior month blocks back-office POSTING — never the till, never biometrics. Capture is always allowed; VERIFICATION is what is withheld (ADR-006 §8) Why: Ian. The checker is adopted as proposed and explains the window better than §7.2 did: the 15 days are the SETTLEMENT period, not slack — an August electricity bill arriving 10 September means August cannot close on 1 September. A recurring-expense template generates a CHECKLIST ITEM, never a posting: the amount varies so it cannot be automated, but the obligation is knowable, which beats auto-posting a figure nobody agreed. I pushed back on the wrong reading and Ian corrected it — I took “block transactions” to include the till; he meant back-office entry, with POS and biometrics running. The one real cost left was that blocking entry does not stop the expense, only its timely recording — trading this month's accuracy for last month's closure. His own sales-day answer generalised solves it: pending-and-unverifiable for all three. Record the draft with its photo while memory is fresh; withhold posting. A growing pile of unpostable drafts is a more legible signal than a greyed-out button, and it is visible to the admin who can act. Daily unlock kept, with a typed reason others can read — friction exercised daily becomes muscle memory by the third day

title: Decision 123 (2026-08-25)
text: close_period requires ORG-WIDE store scope for a manager — the last open matrix cell, now closed. And the OIL integrity-findings layer is PORTED from v1, with one gap fixed: a finding is DERIVED, only the ACKNOWLEDGEMENT is stored (T-135) Why: Ian. The scope answer keeps row 101 and row 114 both true: a period is org-wide, so a Lipa-only manager never closes Malvar's books. On OIL — I assumed “AI insights” meant AI-generated findings and was wrong; integrity.ts says *deterministic* and *pure observation layer, never touches the GL*, and both carry forward unchanged. Second time research has found v1 already at the correct shape. Two of its decisions are better than most systems manage: hardAlert fires through a snooze, closing the snooze-forever escape hatch, and thresholds default in code so a misconfig cannot disable detection. The gap: v1 stores state per finding key, so resolving one suppresses tomorrow's recompute while the condition still holds — the symptom hidden without the cause fixed. Fix: derive the finding, store only the acknowledgement. A finding cannot be resolved while it is still true; acknowledgement means *“seen and accepted for now”*, which is a different and honest statement. That also makes the manager scorecard safe — a score people are measured on is a score people manage, and this removes the way to game it. The close-readiness checker is a FILTER over this feed, not a second engine

title: Decision 124 (2026-08-25)
text: The 31 December cutover is a CONVERSION, not an onboarding wizard — and research corrected three of my own draft's decisions: ordering narrows to FOUR named gates, the REHEARSAL flag is dropped, and the opening entry is a mutable DRAFT until posting locks it (T-134, discovery 21) Why: I designed T-134 before researching it, which is backwards, and Ian said so: *“as always research before design.”* The pass found the draft's substance already right and its vocabulary wrong — “wizard/progress bar” pulled toward SaaS onboarding, where the real prior art is Xero's and Odoo's conversion: ~15 hardcoded steps, one correctness gate. Correction 1 — “not startable until prerequisites verify” was too strong. No reference system hard-blocks checklist steps on each other; hard gates live in close/reopen chains. Narrowed to A1→B1 (ADR-009's inversion), C2→C3, C3→C4, C4→C5 — everything else free-orderable. Correction 2 — no rehearsal flag. No system ships a rehearsal mode inside the live product; every one uses an isolated copy, which ADR-007 already provides, and ADR-007 §1 already rejected per-row markers for this exact reason: a flag is a marker a code path can forget to set. Correction 3 — C3 is a draft until C5 posts it. Xero and Odoo both treat the opening entry as editable until an explicit lock; forcing a formal reversal to fix a typo in a never-final document is ceremony, not control. Also added: an opening-count variance posts against 3900, NEVER 5400 — v2 has no December P&L, so

title: Decision 125 (2026-08-25)
text: A DRAFT expense is DELETED, and deleting it is governed by the EDIT capabilities — no new capability. And the 3900 halt stands, but the opening entry shows a RUNNING residual while you type (T-122 invariant 17, T-134) Why: Ian: *“delete for simplicity.”* Correct, and it closes a real hole — voidExpense refuses a draft (*“nothing has been posted yet to void”*) and nothing discarded one, so a mistaken draft had no ending at all. The justification is narrow and worth stating so it is never widened: a draft is not a financial record — no entry, no balance touched, nobody asserted it. Everything posted is still reversed, never removed. The capability choice is the interesting half: deleting a draft is the LAST EDIT you can make to it, so it reuses edit_own_expense / edit_any_expense rather than minting a delete_expense. There is no coherent answer under which a person may rewrite every field of a draft but not remove it (row 120), and reusing the pair means the 48-hour window cannot drift, because there is only one window. A cashier undoes their own mistake without finding a manager — friction on a self-correction is exactly what produces the abandoned drafts. On the halt: Ian asked whether to mirror the field, where Xero, Odoo and GnuCash all auto-plug an imbalance to suspense. Keep the halt — but the plug account buys those vendors TWO things and only one is bad. It makes the residual *visible* (good) and it makes the residual *postable* (bad). So C3 shows a running difference w

title: Decision 126 (2026-08-25)
text: An UNVERIFIED sales day records no revenue. A new sales report cannot be created while an older one is still unverified. And the entry dates on the SALES DAY, never the posting date (T-123) Why: Ian, answering the three-part question. Verification is what posts — a sales figure nobody checked is exactly what verification exists to catch, so an unverified day is a document, not an entry. The second half is his, and it is better than what I proposed. I suggested only dating on the business date, which fixes the period but lets an unverified day sit for weeks. Blocking a new report while an older one is unverified bounds the lag structurally — the pile cannot grow past one, so revenue is *hours* late rather than days, and the person who must act finds out immediately because they cannot do their next job until they do. A forcing function beats a reminder, and it is the same shape as row 122's unpostable-drafts pile: make the consequence immediate and visible to the person who can clear it. Dating on the sales day then puts a 31 December sale recorded on 2 January into December, where it happened — without which the block would merely relocate the error. Together the two rules make the close honest: the period cannot silently accumulate unrecognised revenue, and nothing lands in the wrong month

title: Decision 127 (2026-08-25)
text: Ian's cash-account OWNER split (cashier / office, each holding cash AND online) is retained — and v2 currently loses half of it: online has NO owner dimension at all Why: Ian: *“the accounts have 2 owners, cashier and office, and cashier has cash and online accounts… this will clearly show money movement.”* The model is right and answers the question a till reconciliation actually asks — whose hands is this money in. The gap, found checking rather than assuming: v2's chart keeps the split for cash (1110 cashier, 1120 staff custodian, 1130 office) but 1140 “E-wallet / online channels” is ONE control subdivided by PROVIDER, with no owner — so *“how much online money is in the cashier's hands versus the office's”* is unanswerable in v2 today. v1 does carry it, as owner?: 'cashier' \

title: Decision 128 (2026-08-25)
text: Remittance may be POOLED across days — but the till is still COUNTED daily, and remittance stops being a field on the sales day. Plus a store revolving fund, which v1 does not have at all (T-136) Why: Ian asked whether remittance could follow the monthly-lock-plus-15-days pattern so three days, a week or a month could go in one remittance. Yes on pooling, and it is safer than it sounds: revenue recognition does not depend on remittance — a sale is revenue when it happens, wherever the cash sits, and remittance only moves money between two ASSET accounts. So pooling cannot make the books wrong. But the cadence must NOT be patterned on the close. The lock's 15 days exist for late-arriving invoices; cash custody is a different risk with a different clock — month-plus-grace means up to 45 days of cash in a drawer, and a shortage found then is attributable to nobody. The resolution keeps both: separate the COUNT from the TRANSFER. Count and hand over the till daily — POS already does exactly this in cashHandovers with expected/counted/variance — and physically remit on whatever cadence suits. The control Ian would be giving up is one he is not actually giving up, because it lives in a different document that keeps running daily. This independently requires the cash-in-transit account row 127 flagged as missing from the unrelated online-owner direction — two needs pointing at one missing account. Structural blocker: v1 stores remittance as FIELDS ON THE SALES DAY (actualRemittanceC

title: Decision 129 (2026-08-25)
text: Remittance cadence is PER STORE, and an un-remitted CEILING forces a remittance regardless of where the cycle is. The mechanism is settled; the peso numbers are Ian's, per store (T-136 §4) Why: Ian: *“yes per store.”* Right — a branch two minutes from the office and one an hour away have genuinely different logistics, so a single global cadence would be wrong for at least one of them. Consequence: cadence is a configuration ROW, never a constant — and a store with none configured must not silently mean “never”. Default to daily, the safe end, and what every store does today; an unset cadence is the same defect class as an unmapped expense category. Per-store cadence makes the ceiling MORE necessary, not less — a store on a weekly cadence accumulates seven days of cash, and ₱200/day versus ₱20,000/day is the same number of days and a completely different amount sitting in a drawer. The risk is the AMOUNT, not the days, so the pooled balance is watched continuously and crossing the ceiling forces a remittance mid-cycle — the same shape as row 122's checker, which watches the condition rather than only the deadline. “Forces” means what it means everywhere else here: the pile becomes visible and unignorable to the person who can clear it, never a blocked till. A cashier is never stopped from selling because a remittance is overdue (discovery 22 §4). I settled the mechanism and deliberately did NOT pick the numbers — a peso ceiling and an imprest amount are business policy, and th

title: Decision 130 (2026-08-25)
text: POS TRANSACTS, ERP ACCOUNTS. The cash handover folds to the ERP — one computation, one owner. And platform sales (Foodpanda / Grab) stay MANUALLY entered, because their own terminals are the system of record (discovery 23, T-123 §7) Why: Ian: *“for v2 POS will only transact — its job is getting the order, passing order to kitchen and server, computing and processing payment. Just that. ERP will handle the money: where it goes, is it used in operations, remitted to manager etc. POS frontend, ERP backend.”* The existing configuration already sorts almost perfectly along that line (discovery 23 §3), which is a good sign the split is natural rather than imposed. On the handover, his reason is the decisive one and it is better than “pick one to avoid duplication”: POS computes expectedCash = startingCash + cashSales − deductions[], but POS does not know the deductions — a cashier-paid expense, a released cash request, an online-to-cash conversion, an AP payment from the till are every one of them ERP documents. So POS's deductions[] can only be filled by the cashier re-entering what the ERP already knows — a second entry point for one fact, which is exactly how two figures come to disagree. An expected-cash figure is only as good as its deduction data, and only one system has it. POS may still take the physical count at the drawer, but it submits evidence, it does not compute expected cash. Design for, do not discover: POS sells offline and the ERP may be unreachable at shift chan

title: Decision 131 (2026-08-25)
text: The cash-custody research: the account is UNDEPOSITED FUNDS (I had the term wrong), the till reconciles PER CASHIER PER SHIFT with denomination counts, v1's less/plus is AHEAD of ERPNext — and a mandatory per-transaction PWD/senior LOGBOOK exists that nothing captures today (discovery 24) Why: Correction first: I wrote “cash in transit / undeposited funds” in rows 127 and 128 as if interchangeable and they are not. *Undeposited funds* is our books versus where the money physically is; *deposit in transit* is our books versus the bank's — a bank-reconciliation timing item with nothing to do with a till. Using the wrong one would have invited someone to reconcile a till against a bank statement. Row 129's ceiling is retro-justified by the field: vendors describe batched deposits as the ordinary case for undeposited funds, AND warn it is *“one of the accounts most likely to cause a business's financial statements to be incorrect”* because money piles up in it forever when the deposit step is never done. A pooled-remittance design without a ceiling is that failure with extra steps. From ERPNext's POS Opening/Closing Entry, three things to adopt: reconciliation per cashier per shift (v1 is per store per day, which cannot attribute a variance when two cashiers worked — and attribution is the whole custody control), denomination-level counting (quantity of each note and coin, not one total), and expected/closing/difference PER PAYMENT METHOD, which is row 127's owner/instrument spli

title: Decision 132 (2026-08-25)
text: Senior/PWD discounts stay CONTRA-REVENUE (4900). The till reconciles PER SHIFT and the sales day stays PER DAY — both, not one. And the statutory discount LOGBOOK becomes a requirement: ~~today only the ID is captured~~ — THAT HALF IS FALSE, corrected by row 164 Why: Ian, answering discovery 24's three opens. One reading stated rather than assumed: he answered *“contra asset”*, and I am taking that as contra-REVENUE — the choice on the table was contra-revenue (4900, current) versus BIR's *“Expenses – PWD Discounts”*, and *contra* is the operative half. A sales discount is not a contra-asset (that class is accumulated depreciation, allowance for doubtful accounts — a valuation account against something the business owns). So 4900 stands unchanged and POSTING-PATTERNS.md's sale.discount.senior-pwd needs no edit. If he meant something else this is the line to correct. Per shift AND per day is the right answer and it settles T-123 §3's decomposition: the till position (split B) is per cashier per shift, which is what makes a variance attributable to one person; the sales day (split A) stays per store per day, which is what revenue recognition and the period close need. Shifts roll up into a day — they are not competing grains, they are two levels of one hierarchy, and v1 already carries both (its derive-totals.ts branches on whether it is writing a shift doc or a day doc). ~~On the logbook: today the business captures only the ID.~~ CORRECTED BY ROW 164 — nothing captures an ID

title: Decision 133 (2026-08-25)
text: totalSales is the SUM OF ALL CHANNELS, remitted and non-remitted together — and v1's sales report DERIVES almost everything from a small input set, where mine asks the user to type figures that must agree. My form has the shape wrong (T-123, derive-totals.ts) Why: Ian: *“see how the current sales report doc looks — total sales are all sales channel sum, remitted daily and un-remitted daily combined.”* Confirmed at source: totalSales = channelsTotal + branchDelta, where channelsTotal is Σ of every channel. I never enforced that, so my own browser smoketest passed a day whose channels summed to ₱550 against a ₱6,000 total — the identity I omitted is exactly the one that would have caught it. The bigger finding is the INPUT model, and v1's is better than mine by construction. v1 takes per-channel amounts, a per-account online breakdown, credit and other tenders, and auto-queries the cashier's less/plus — then derives totalSales, cashPayments, the remittance expectations and the rest. Cash is DERIVED (remitted channels − online − credit − other), never typed. So the figures cannot disagree with each other, because only one set is entered. Mine asks for total, unli, à la carte, cash and online as five independent numbers and then checks they agree — which makes a data-entry error possible where v1 makes it impossible. Two further details worth keeping: cashierAccountIds decides which online accounts count, because *“online sales into any other account are not the cashier's to remi

title: Decision 134 (2026-08-25)
text: v2 records GROSS with discounts AND charges on their own lines. And the two kinds of “charge” are OPPOSITE: service charge is a LIABILITY (2160, RA 11360), other charges are INCOME (4500) (T-123) Why: Ian, in two steps. First: *“when the ERP pulls sales from POS it's NET, not gross, so discounts and charges are accounted”* — which describes v1. Then: *“but for v2 I agree it's better to include discounts and charges in the sales report so they both have clear lines and the data can easily be used.”* So totalSales is gross food revenue and every adjustment to it is a line somebody can read, rather than a number already absorbed into another number. The consequential half is the charge split, and Ian's own framing found it: *“we charge leftover charge, packaging charge and other charges — I want them all in ONE account, separated from service charge.”* Separating them turns out to be far more than tidiness. RA 11360 sends 100% of service charge to rank-and-file employees, at least twice a month, so the business collects it as an agent and keeps none of it — it is a payable from the moment it is taken, not income. Leftover and packaging charges the business does keep, so those really are income. Two things that look identical on a bill and sit on opposite sides of the balance sheet. The asymmetry decides it even before an accountant confirms: booking service charge as income overstates profit AND hides a payable, and it does not self-correct; the reverse error self-corrects the m

title: Decision 135 (2026-08-25)
text: Service charge is a FLOAT at 2160 — neither revenue nor accounts payable. It touches the balance sheet only and never the P&L. This SUPERSEDES row 134's liability-vs-income framing (T-123) Why: Three passes, and Ian rejected two treatments for two different and correct reasons before landing here. (1) *“It will go with the salary and later be expensed, so it must be collection first, revenue first — don't push to accounts payable.”* The AP half is right and worth stating: AP is money owed to SUPPLIERS, with a party, an age and a payment process, and this is none of those. (2) Then, on his own proposal: *“but it will bloat the revenue.”* Also right — ₱1M of food plus ₱100k of service charge would read as ₱1.1M of income, ₱100k of which was never the business's money. (3) *“Let it not touch accounting? How do other platforms handle it?”* It cannot be kept out entirely, and the reason is physical: the cash enters the drawer. ₱1,100 tendered on a ₱1,000 bill leaves ₱1,100 in the till, so books recording ₱1,000 never reconcile against a count. It must land somewhere; the float is the treatment that touches accounting least — balance sheet only, self-clearing. The research settles it, and the field's dividing line is WHOSE MONEY IT IS, not what the bill calls it: tips are voluntary and belong to staff, so they go to a liability clearing account (“Tips Payable”) cleared through payroll; service charges elsewhere are the RESTAURANT's money to distribute or not, so they are revenue wi

title: Decision 136 (2026-08-25)
text: The service-charge float is DISTRIBUTED on a per-store cadence — and MONTHLY IS NOT LAWFUL, so the setting must not be able to express it (T-136 §6) Why: Ian: *“yes we float it, and distribute per day, per week or per month.”* The float is settled (row 135); this is how it empties. Daily and weekly are fine. Monthly is not: RA 11360 requires distribution at least twice a month, at intervals not exceeding sixteen days, so a monthly cadence is a breach by construction rather than by accident. The design consequence is the interesting part: the configuration must not be able to hold the wrong answer. Same instinct as is_remitted_daily being NOT NULL with no default — if a setting can be set to something unlawful, eventually it will be, and nobody notices, because a float that keeps growing reads as a healthy balance rather than an overdue obligation. So an ageing 2160 is a FINDING, not a balance — it belongs in the OIL feed (T-135) as *“service charge float older than 16 days”*, derived from the condition so it cannot be resolved while still true. It shares its shape with the remittance cadence (row 129) and deliberately NOT its number: both are per-store cash movements on a configurable rhythm, but remittance is bounded by how much cash you are willing to hold in a drawer and this one is bounded by STATUTE. title: Decision 139 (2026-08-26)
text: Capitalisation threshold raised to ₱10,000, and useful lives become PER CATEGORY — the question a life answers is “when would we REPLACE it”, not “how long could it last” (T-124, discovery 25) Why: Ian: *“let's raise it to 10k”*, then *“what's with building being 20 and vehicle 5 — what is logical to assign?”* The threshold is a materiality judgement with a physical cost here: every capitalised item is a row someone must stand in front of during T-134's December walk-round, so doubling it removes the cheap end of the register. A timing difference, not a permanent one — a ₱8,000 rice cooker reaches the P&L on the day it is bought instead of over five years. Where the number lives matters as much as the number: v1 reads it from config and REFUSES TO POST if it cannot be read, because a silent fallback *“understates depreciation by ~60%”* — ported exactly. On the lives, the reasoning is the durable part and the numbers are not: a life answers *“how long until we would realistically replace this?”*, never *“how long could it last?”* — the second is a manufacturer's brochure, the first is what makes depreciation match reality. Three drivers: physical wear (a commercial kitchen is brutal — the same fridge lasts far longer in an office), obsolescence (replaced because something better exists), and AESTHETIC life — replaced because the place looks tired, which is the one most businesses forget to price and the reason restaurant furniture is retired long before it breaks. title: Decision 140 (2026-08-26)
text: A useful life is a COUNT OF MONTHS, defaulting to 24 — this supersedes row 139's per-category table of years. Depreciation posts PER ASSET per period, and the interval is chosen when the asset is added, from monthly / quarterly / SEMI-ANNUAL / annual (T-124) Why: Ian, answering all three of T-124 §11's open questions at once: *“default to 24 months make configurable by months”*, *“per asset per period”*, *“for period when asset is added user may configure monthly quarterly semi anual annual”*. Row 139's REASONING survives; its unit and its owner do not. “How long until we would realistically REPLACE it” is still the right question — what changed is that it is answered per asset, in months, by the person adding it, not once per category in years by an accountant. That also retires row 139's open “wants the accountant's nod”, because there is no longer a table to nod at. Years could not express the answer. A 30-month life rounds to 2 or 3 in years, and a silent rounding of the very estimate depreciation is built on is exactly what §6 refuses elsewhere for money. So useful_life_years becomes useful_life_months; asset_category_lives survives as a per-category DEFAULT, in months, seeded to 24 across the board so a category can be given its own later without a migration. Semi-annual is genuinely new — absent from the schema enum, its CHECK constraint and schedule.ts's interval map. Migration 0019 is already applied, so this lands as a NEW migration (§2 rule 8). title: Decision 141 (2026-08-26)
text: The capitalisation threshold drops to ₱5,000 — back to v1's figure — and ONE threshold now governs fixed assets AND prepaid items. This SUPERSEDES row 139's ₱10,000. (T-124, T-125) Why: Ian: *“we seldomly use that prepaid capital and i suggest both asset and prepaid must be lowered to 5k since 10k might be a bit high to absorb in one accounting period.”* The reasoning runs the opposite way to intuition, and he has it the right way round. A HIGHER threshold does not spread more cost — it expenses more of it immediately, because everything BELOW the line is absorbed in one period. ₱10,000 was therefore the setting that allowed a ₱9,999 purchase to land entirely in one month's P&L. Lowering to ₱5,000 sends more purchases into a schedule instead. What row 139 traded away, and is now being traded back. 139 raised the figure for materiality, and its cost was physical: every asset over the line is a row somebody stands in front of during the December walk-round (T-134 B2). Lowering it means MORE rows to count in December and a busier needs_review queue, since auto-capitalisation from a CAPEX expense flags every asset it creates. That is the accepted cost, not an oversight. ONE threshold, deliberately. v1 kept two — appConfig/capitalization (org-level) for assets and stores/{id}/financialConfig/thresholds (store-scoped) for prepaid — the same default by coincidence, different scope, never reconciled, and v1's own ACCOUNTING_BLUEPRINT still lists the split as unresolved. v2 has one va

title: Decision 142 (2026-08-26)
text: ADR-010 ACCEPTED — ONE ledger, TWO views. Ownership belongs to the PLACE money sits, never to the transaction. Custodians are cashier · office · staff, a money account is per ACCOUNT not per provider, and 1120 must become party-required. This CLOSES row 127's research pass. Why: Ian framed it and the framing was the answer: *“we do 2 levels of accounting here — the general one, business-wide, where all cash whoever the owner is is business cash … and the other level curated to our needs, the one with these owners … for internal only. How can we model it cleanly?”* They are not two sets of books. A line records WHERE money is; who holds it is an attribute of that place. The general view groups lines by account, the internal view groups the SAME lines by the place's attributes. Two views over one set of lines cannot disagree — two ledgers always eventually do, and v1 is proving it in the live books: AP control ₱669,829.84 against a subledger of ₱1,567,980.87, and 34 of 115 account/store combinations disagreeing with a reconstruction from raw legs. The rule that decides account-vs-attribute is a test, not taste: does it get reconciled against something outside the books? A drawer is counted, a safe is counted, each wallet has a statement — accounts. Nobody reconciles “the cashier” against an external document — attribute. Ownership fails the test, which is exactly why DEF-058's *“the owner belongs to the ACCOUNT, derived never ticked”* is right. Asking for a third custodian expo

title: Decision 143 (2026-08-26)
text: UNDEPOSITED FUNDS needs NO account — it is a DERIVED state, the balance of every cashier-custodian account. And the till is a MIXED POT, so expected cash is not today's sales. This closes rows 127 and 131's last open item. Why: Ian: *“currently we treat that as cash cashier or cashier online — so cashier cash is composed [of] sales made today and all other collections made by cashier, like receivables from past days, return of staff from cash request. Cash from sales sitting on till is cash cashier; online payments from sales is cashier online.”* Rows 127 and 131 assumed “v1 has no account for undeposited funds” was a GAP to fill. It is not — v1 is right. §2's test says why: nobody reconciles “undeposited funds” against an external document; they reconcile the TILL, and the till is 1110. Money is undeposited precisely while it sits in a cashier-custodian account, so the figure is sum(balance) where custodian='cashier' — a GROUP BY over the ledger, not a posting. ADR-010's model answers a question it was not designed for, and adding the account would have created a second place the same pesos are recorded, which is the exact failure ADR-010 §1 exists to prevent. Row 129's peso ceiling applies to the derived figure. The second half matters more. The till is a MIXED POT: today's cash sales, PLUS collections on past-day receivables, PLUS returned staff floats, LESS cash paid out of the drawer. So “expected cash” ≠ “today's sales cash”, and a reconciliation built on that equation

title: Decision 144 (2026-08-26)
text: A pooled remittance settles the days it covers OLDEST FIRST, and the variance lands on the last date because that is where FIFO puts it. But a batch shortage is a CUSTODY variance, not a COUNT variance — date it on the last day, attribute it to whoever HELD the pool. (T-136 §7) Why: Ian: *“each sales day locks on verified so all remittable cash and online is recorded, but remittance may happen by batch — Lipa has 5 sitting sales reports for January 1 to 5, all verified … it can be remitted all at once … if the remittance is short, cover the oldest sales report first, and record shortage/overage on the last date.”* The daily lock is row 128's COUNT; the batch is its TRANSFER, so this is that decision's allocation rule rather than a new one. “Record it on the last date” is not an extra convention — it is what FIFO produces, and a rule that falls out of the allocation cannot drift from it. The refinement, from evaluating it: once the till is counted and signed daily, a batch shortage cannot be a counting error — the counts already reconciled. It is a loss in CUSTODY, after the fact, and therefore a different question asked of a possibly different person. So dating it on the last date is right and attributing it to that date's cashier is not: the last date is where the arithmetic puts the residual, and says nothing about who was holding the money. v1 already refuses to guess — its remittance builder THROWS if a shortage posts without an explicit chargeToStaffId — and that refusal

title: Decision 145 (2026-08-26)
text: Expected remittance is the cashier accounts' NET MOVEMENT, derived from the ledger — not a sum over document types. Ian's inventory of ins and outs is the DOCUMENTATION of what posts there, never the computation. (T-136 §8) Why: Ian: *“today's remittance = all money in less all money out touched by cashier. In: sales, collections, returns, refunds from vendors. Out: expense with payment from cashier (cashier's part only, not necessarily the whole expense amount), cash request released by cashier, salary advance released by cashier, payment to payables by cashier, other out to be determined.”* Checked all eight against the worked examples, no exceptions: money IN is a debit to a cashier-custodian account, money OUT is a credit. So expected = Σdebits − Σcredits where custodian='cashier', over the period being remitted — row 143's “derived, not maintained” applied one level up. “Other out to be determined” is the tell for why the list must NOT be implemented as a list. Summed over enumerated document types, that phrase is a live hole: any transaction touching the till and missing from the enumeration silently breaks the reconciliation, in the direction that makes a cashier look short. DEF-044's shape again — a figure maintained beside the ledger rather than read from it. Derived from the account, *other out* needs no determining: anything crediting the cashier's account is already counted, including transaction types nobody has thought of yet, because posting IS registering. And

text: Batch remittance is ADDITIVE — daily remittance is not replaced — and a partially-settled day displays as partially_remitted, which v1 already has. Correcting my own claim that it did not. (T-136 §7.5) Why: Ian: *“the unsettled sales day displays as partially remitted just like v1.
