title: Decision 147 (2026-08-26)
text: An unsettled remittance does NOT block the next one — it gets its OWN TABLE so it cannot hide. The table holds the CASE and its lifecycle; the peso figure stays DERIVED. (T-136 §7.6) Why: Ian: *“no it won't block, but it must be flagged and dedicate a separate table so it won't hide from sight like v1 does.”* Not blocking is right — a shortage on Jan 5 is no reason to strand Jan 6–10's cash in a drawer, which would make the control cause the very risk it exists to reduce. And “like v1 does” is evidenced, not a hunch: v1 proves it against itself. Row 146 records the admin button v1 had to build for days *“stuck on partially_remitted even though all transfers are posted”*. A stuck status that needed a repair tool is a status nobody was watching — rendered in a column, in a list, among days that all looked alike. Visible without being seen. A table is exactly right for the flag and exactly wrong for the figure. How much is outstanding stays DERIVED (expected per row 145, less what remittances have settled) — a stored balance is a second place the same pesos live, which rows 143 and 145 both refuse. What the table holds is what is NOT derivable: that a case exists, who owns it, when it was raised, what was decided, whether it is closed. A human process needs a record; a number does not. The table can never disagree with the books because it holds no number that could. Three states, and conflating them is the trap: *outstanding* (counted, signed, not handed over yet — nobody is an

title: Decision 148 (2026-08-26)
text: ONE split-payment shape for every money movement, each line naming its ACCOUNT and DIRECTION — and sales come in from POS already split, because POS is where the customer's payment mode is captured. (DEF-068, ADR-010) Why: Ian: *“the cashier POS has this — it defines which mode of payment is used by customer … so for sales transaction it will go in from POS, and POS on billing screen has split payment; for other transaction it is ERP split payment. Both work — we introduce a dropdown picker to dictate direction and account.”* This answers ADR-010's last practical obstacle. Attributing online money needs 1140 to require a party, and the blocker was that a sales day had nothing to supply — one online_collected figure, no wallet. It turns out the data was never missing: POS captures it at the till and v1 already carries it (sale.builder.ts takes onlineBreakdown: Record<accountId, amount> and posts one leg per account). T-123 simply did not carry it across — registered as DEF-068. The axis confusion worth naming once: a CHANNEL is not a PAYMENT ACCOUNT. sales_day_channels records where a sale came FROM (Walk-in, Foodpanda — revenue and receivables); a payment account records where the money WENT (custody). They are orthogonal — a Foodpanda sale can settle into any wallet — and v2 modelled the first while dropping the second. The unifying decision: one split shape everywhere, each line naming a money account and a direction, so a POS-sourced sale and a hand-entered AP payment desc

title: Decision 149 (2026-08-26)
text: ONLY AN ADMIN MAY ADD AN ACCOUNT TO THE BOOKS — a standing rule, not a decision about one screen. The gate is manage_chart_of_accounts (org-scoped, admin and super-admin only). Why: Ian: *“only admin can add accounts to the books”* … *“that must be the rule.”* Recorded because I got it wrong first, and the wrong reasoning is the instructive part. I gated money_accounts on manage_store_settings — manager-and-above, store-scoped — on the grounds that a branch manager adding the store's GCash account is ordinary configuration. It is not configuration. A money account IS an account in the books: every peso entering it lands on the balance sheet under a GL code, and creating one creates a place money can be attributed to. That is the same act as adding a chart-of-accounts row and belongs at the same level. The rule generalises past this table, which is why it is a row and not a code comment. Anything that creates a place money or value can be recorded against — a money account today, a bank account, a new control account, a category that mints its own GL row — is an admin act. A manager RECORDS transactions; only an admin changes what the books can record them against. A wallet is per-store while the capability is per-ORG, and that is correct rather than sloppy: the store says where the money sits; the authority to open a new place for money to sit is the org's. An admin already holds org-wide scope, so nothing is widened. Retiring one is the same authority as creating it — it cha

title: Decision 150 (2026-08-26)
text: MOVING money between accounts is MANAGER level; OPENING one stays admin-only. New capability transfer_funds (store-scoped, manager and up). Why: Ian: *“yes manager level money transfer.”* The pairing with row 149 is the decision, not the level. Row 149 made adding an account admin-only because it changes *what the books can record against*. A transfer changes nothing about the books' shape — it RECORDS something that already happened to money that is already there. Those are different acts and they earn different levels. The concrete test: a manager may already accept_remittance, which is the single largest transfer this business makes (a whole day's takings, cashier to office). Barring that same manager from moving ₱500 between two drawers would be incoherent. transfer_funds is manager-TRUE, so it does NOT join ELEVATED_GRANTS_FOR_ADMINLESS_MANAGER — that set is derived as admin-yes/manager-no, and a manager holds this one outright. Nothing to grant, nothing to remember. Adding it forced edits to CAPABILITY-MATRIX.md, capabilities.ts and three pinned counts (38 → 39) — that friction is the guard working: a capability cannot reach the enforcement without also reaching the document people read.

title: Decision 151 (2026-08-26)
text: A TRANSFER STATES BOTH AMOUNTS — what left AND what arrived. The fee is DERIVED, never entered or stored. (T-139 §3) Why: Found by two of our own sources disagreeing. v1's builder takes one amount meaning *what arrives* and charges the source amount + fee; POSTING-PATTERNS.md's worked example narrates the same three legs the other way round, as *“a ₱10,000 transfer that costs ₱50, so only ₱9,950 lands.”* The posted legs are identical either way — which is exactly why nobody noticed — but the same figure typed in the same box produces two different transfers. And both readings are real here: a bank wire ADDS its fee to the source (send ₱10,000, get debited ₱10,050); a GCash cash-out DEDUCTS it from the target (cash out ₱10,000, receive ₱9,950). So the answer is to refuse the convention entirely rather than pick one and document it. Both figures are observable facts — one on each statement being reconciled — which is what makes a transfer checkable at all, and the fee is whatever went missing between them. No fee column, and amount_in > amount_out is refused: money that arrives without leaving somewhere is income, not a transfer.

title: Decision 152 (2026-08-26)
text: MONEY MOVES BETWEEN STORES OFFICE TO OFFICE ONLY — a cashier or staff account at either end is REFUSED. And no transfer may overdraw its source. Why: Ian, describing what actually happens: *“a manager of lipa and malvar who is not allowed to get remittance is able to collect money from malvar to spend on lipa — but that’s deeply wrong. The right pattern is malvar remits to office first before lipa can use it.”* The rule is about the CUSTODIAN, not the store, and that is the whole insight. The abuse is someone reaching into another store’s till; banning cross-store movement outright would be wrong because the business genuinely needs it. Forcing it through the office makes the bypass unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged — and it restores the control that was being sidestepped, since remittance is exactly the step a manager without accept_remittance was skipping. The receiving end must be an office too, so one due-from/due-to pair covers each movement; the destination store then moves it onward with an ordinary same-store transfer. This cost almost nothing to build because the shape already existed: 1250 Due from / 2150 Due to related store, party_type='store' carrying the other store’s CODE, and bible invariant 6’s reciprocal check — the same four legs commissary_dispatch.transfer posts for inventory, with cash in place of goods. Still unbuilt, and the larger half of Ian’s scenario: Malvar office cash funding a cash request whose liquidated expense belongs to Lipa, w

title: Decision 153 (2026-08-26)
text: CROSS-STORE MONEY MOVEMENT REQUIRES STORE ACCESS TO *BOTH* STORES — and this is a rule about the MOVEMENT, not about the screen it was reached through. It applies to transfers today and to cash requests when they are built. And no expense may overdraw the account that funds it, checked at APPROVE. Why: Ian: *“cross store money movement will only be possible for manager initiated transactions, with manager having access like hasStoreAccess to both stores”*, and *“yes extend”* (the overdraw block, from transfers to expenses). Authorising only the SOURCE store was a real hole — the same abuse as row 152 seen from the other side: a manager scoped to Malvar alone could push Malvar's money into Lipa, a store they have no standing in, and Lipa would find money it never asked for and now owes for. authorize() already checks personHasStoreScope per call, so a second call IS the rule — no new helper, and the denial names the missing store. The reason this is framed as being about the movement: an expense at Lipa paid from Malvar's safe moves Malvar's money exactly as a transfer does. Gating transfers alone would have left the identical act reachable one menu across, so approveExpense applies the same check whenever a payment names an account belonging to another store. On overdraw, expenses were the surface that actually needed it: expense payment is ~34% of ledger activity against a transfer's 7%, so a drawer is far likelier to go negative through spending than through moving money. title: Decision 154 (2026-08-26)
text: OVERDRAFT IS A PROPERTY OF THE ACCOUNT, NOT OF THE FEATURE. A CASHIER account is WARNED and still posts; an OFFICE or STAFF account is REFUSED. Supersedes row 153's blanket block. Why: Ian, on the ordering hazard row 153 raised: *“warning for now, don’t block … implement it only to cashier owned account, since only cashier owned account might experience this.”* This is a better rule than the blanket warning I offered, and the reason is worth keeping: a cashier account holds money the ledger genuinely cannot see yet, because a sales day posts only at verify — a drawer reading ₱0 at 2pm may hold ₱40,000. Refusing there refuses a shortfall that is not real, and nothing drives people to work around a system faster than being told they have no money while they are looking at it. No other custodian has that gap: an office safe or a staff float only ever receives money through a transfer, cash request or liquidation, all of which post the moment they happen — so its balance is COMPLETE, a negative is a real error, and it stays refused. The rule therefore turns on custodian, never on which screen the money left through, which is why it lives in ONE file (money-accounts/overdraft.ts) that both approveExpense and createMoneyTransfer call. Two copies of this decision would drift exactly as v1's two amortisation runners did. A warning nobody sees is v1's disease, so it surfaces twice: returned from the service at the moment of posting, and shown standing on the money-transfers screen as

title: Decision 155 (2026-08-27)
text: ONE AUTH TENANT (shareat-hub-v2), AND STORAGE SPLIT BY SENSITIVITY — NOT BY APP. ERP staff sign in with the same Firebase identity they use in POS. Public CDN content stays in the world-readable default bucket; accounting documents go in a separate private bucket, reached only through the Admin SDK. v2 never deploys Storage or Firestore rules. Why: Ian: *“yes same firebase identity as POS — that’s the whole point of the system we are building, we will combine the backend of these separate apps as much as possible, so 1 auth yes”*, and *“storage can be separated yes, since POS and CUSTOMER app are public facing the menu photo must not be strictly accessed.”* The split is by what the FILE is, not by which app wrote it, and that is the whole insight. shareat-hub-v2’s bucket is allow read; — no condition, world-readable, unauthenticated — which is CORRECT for menu photos, logos and loyalty images served to diners, and would be catastrophic for supplier invoices. POS already hit this and could not fix it: its own rules note that for customer payment proofs *“Storage rules OR across matching blocks, so a stricter allow read accomplishes nothing”*, leaving them to rely on an unguessable UUID path and a 15-day lifecycle delete. Receipt photos are not payment proofs — they carry suppliers, prices and volumes, and they are kept for years, so security-by-unguessable-URL is not an accounting control. Putting the private bucket in the SAME project as Auth avoids a cross-project service-ac

title: Decision 156 (2026-08-26)
text: EVERY STORE IS BORN WITH FIVE MONEY ACCOUNTS, AND CANNOT CLOSE THEM WHILE IT TRADES. Cashier cash · cashier online · office cash · office online · staff float. Names are editable; the shape is not. Why: Ian: *“all stores must have these accounts, seeded and configurable but can never be terminated as long as store is active … these 5 accounts must always be present and available since they are the foundation of money movement”*, and *“cashier cash may be renamed to counter till, office cash may be office vault … unretirable but configurable in ui esp name.”* Enforced by a TRIGGER on stores, not by a service call, because there is no createStore service: stores arrive from the seed, the ETL, the cutover and one day a screen — four paths, and an invariant should not be a step any of them has to remember. Same reasoning that already put ledger balance and period-open in triggers. And it is load-bearing NOW: since row 150's work a cash payment must NAME a money account, so a store created without these silently cannot record a cash expense at all. is_foundation is a FLAG, not an inference from instrument + custodian, and that is the crux: a store may open a SECOND cashier wallet (another GCash, a bank account) and that one is ordinary — retirable like anything else. Nothing about its shape distinguishes it from the seeded one, so only a flag can. Backfill ADOPTS before it seeds, and only an account that is the store's ONLY active one of that shape: a hand-made “Cashier drawer” ke

title: Decision 157 (2026-08-27)
text: WHAT IS REMITTED IS THE END-DAY REPORT, NOT THE SALES REPORT — and they are ONE thing, not two. A day is owed the CASHIER'S NET MOVEMENT for that date, not its remittable sales. Why: Ian: *“remittance is derived from sales report — they are one, actually. It must be END DAY REPORT, not sales report. The sales report is PART OF that remittance / end-day report… the sales day is sum of sales, collection etc enclosed in same sales day. So for cleaner reporting, the sales-day report generates on POS; the one that is remitted is the remittance or end-day report — the composition of all money movement of the day across transactions.”* This dissolves a gap I had raised as an open question. I had modelled a day as owing its remittable SALES, and asked what to do with the rest of the till — a ₱5,000 collection and a ₱2,000 expense that no sales day is owed. There is no remainder, because the day is not its sales: it is everything the cashier touched. Row 145 (“expected remittance is the cashier accounts’ net movement”) and the FIFO rule (row 144) turn out to be the SAME figure, one totalled and one per date. sales_days is not renamed and does not grow. It stays the POS-sourced SALES component and, critically, the LOCK — a date becomes remittable when its sales day is verified. The end-day report contains it. And the end-day report is DERIVED: the cashier-custodian accounts’ net movement for one store on one date, read from the ledger. No table, no stored expected, and it picks up a ne

title: Decision 158 (2026-08-27)
text: LOANS GET A STANDARD MODEL, NOT v1'S. ONE REGISTER — THE LEDGER — AND THE PRINCIPAL/INTEREST SPLIT IS COMPUTED, NEVER TYPED. Why: Ian: *“that loan model in v1 is really flawed. I suggest build a standard one for loan and we will build on top of it later to cater our case.”* v1 recorded the same debt in THREE places: four running totals on the loan (totalPaid, principalPaid, interestPaid, outstandingBalance — the last commented *“principalAmount - principalPaid”*, a stored copy of a subtraction), a loanPayments collection, and a LoanLedgerEntry carrying its own balanceBefore. They drifted, and it was MEASURED rather than guessed: the ERPNext migration read both live Grab loans and concluded *“NEITHER figure is usable”* — one stale by fourteen days of unrecorded settlements, the other reading zero payments because every settlement routed through a single channelCfg.loanId, *“a wiring artifact, not a fact.”* So there is no loan_payments table: a payment is not a thing beside the ledger, it IS a ledger entry, and giving it a second home is how v1 got three. The party on a 2400 line is THE LOAN, not the lender — which looks like the wrong noun until you ask what a party is for: it makes each balance on a shared control account attributable, and a lender can hold two loans, which v1's own data proves. The split is computed — v1 takes it from the caller with a suggestion the caller may ignore, so the number deciding how fast a debt retires is hand-typed. Interest accrued since the l

title: Decision 159 (2026-08-27)
text: A CASH REQUEST IS A FLOAT THAT MUST NET TO ZERO, AND 1120 GAINS A PARTY — THE REQUEST. ASKING FOR MONEY POSTS NOTHING; ONLY THE RELEASE DOES. Why: Four postings, and only the middle one already existed. Release DR 1120 / CR the funding account; spend DR the expense / CR 1120 — T-122 has done this all along, and expense_payments.cash_request_id says why in its own comment: *“presence alone routes a cash payment to 1120 instead of 1110.”* This task supplied the document that column had been pointing at for six weeks. Return DR the funding account / CR 1120; shortage DR 1230 staff advance / CR 1120. The four net to ZERO when the request closes — which is what distinguishes a float from an imprest fund (T-136 §2 holds a standing balance and is replenished; this holds nothing between requests), and it is why liquidated needs no column. The request itself posts nothing (§16.10): asking is not a financial event, and a system that posted on request would show a float in someone's hands before anyone handed it over. 1120 becomes party-requiring — v1's is not, and POSTING-PATTERNS.md records v1's reasoning verbatim: *“1120 is not a requires_party account — it is a plain asset, not a control account with a subledger.”* And the correction matters, because the obvious version of this argument is wrong: v1 DOES name the holder — requesterName and requesterUid sit on the request document. What v1 cannot do is answer the question from the LEDGER. A store has ONE staff-float account (row 156)

title: Decision 160 (2026-08-27)
text: A PERSONAL EXPENSE IS ROUTED BY WHETHER THE MONEY IS EXPECTED BACK, NOT BY WHO SPENT IT — AND DRAWINGS GET A MONTHLY CLOSE THAT LOCKS THE MONTH. Why: Ian: *“personal expense must be parked at owner's drawing, not automatically posted against it. It might be posted against owner's salary if they are given; if owner's salary does not exist then owner's drawing”*, then after evaluation: *“go to your 2route version, and for drawing can we make monthly close for that too so all drawings within the cut off period is reconciled and recorded properly and acknowledge adjustment if any visible and enforced.”* The three-route cascade was right about ORDER and wrong about TIMING. Cash first, payroll second, equity last is the correct priority — but *“if not paid”* has no date, so nothing can decide at approval that the owner will not pay. Declaring a receivable uncollectible is an act with a date and an author; making it a fallback would have the system invent that date. So the three became SETTLEMENTS of one receivable, not routes. The fact that actually splits it is known on day one: does the business expect the money back? repayable → 1260 Due from owners (🆕); drawing → 3200. And it is the same line the tax treatment turns on — a payment made with no expectation of repayment is a constructive dividend however it is labelled, which is why the choice is a stated policy per owner rather than a guess at posting time. The drawing limit counts 1260 AND 3200, and that is load-bearing: a cap

title: Decision 161 (2026-08-27)
text: A CASHIER DRAWER'S OVERDRAFT IS CAPPED, PER ACCOUNT, AND ADMIN SETS IT. ROW 154's WARNING NOW HAS A FLOOR. Why: Ian: *“how deep can a cashier account be negative — it can't be unlimited, so admin can set it. If the set is 20,000 that is the only allowable negative balance a cashier is allowed to.”* Row 154's reasoning was right and had no floor of its own. A till's true balance is unknowable until the day is verified — the cash is in the drawer before it is in the ledger — so a shortfall is a *“look at this”*, not a *“you are wrong”*. But that argument justifies a drawer being ₱2,000 behind and equally ₱2,000,000 behind. The first is a bookkeeping lag; the second is a missing drawer, and nothing in the ledger could tell them apart. The cap is where *“legitimately behind”* stops. money_accounts.overdraft_limit, stored POSITIVE, default ₱20,000 — Ian's own example, and a starting value rather than a policy. Zero is meaningful: it means that drawer may never go below zero at all, which is why a blank field on the form means *“leave it alone”* and not *“set it to zero”*. The test is where the balance LANDS, not how big the draw is. A ₱105,000 draw against a ₱100,000 drawer leaves it ₱5,000 behind and passes; a ₱1,000 draw against a drawer already ₱19,500 behind is what breaches a ₱20,000 cap. Judging the draw would refuse the first wrongly and allow the second. PER ACCOUNT, not per org, and that is deliberate: a busier store carries a bigger float, so a single org-wide number wou

title: Decision 162 (2026-08-27)
text: AGING IS BY DUE DATE, NOT INVOICE DATE, FOR BOTH AP AND AR. Why: Ian: *“due date.”* An invoice or charge with no stated due date (informal supplier or customer terms — real, not hypothetical) falls back to its own document date for aging only; the fallback does not change which basis governs when a due date exists. §16.10 requires ONE basis held across AP and AR, so this is decided once here rather than re-litigated per module — T-131 (AR) must use it. Drafted in docs/tasks/130-accounts-payable.md Invariant 11 on 2026-08-27 and left unlanded, because the implementer was Sonnet and §14 reserves amendments to the planner; it sat as an explicit unrecorded item across two handoffs before an Opus pass landed it on 2026-08-28. That delay is the rule working, not failing — but a decision waiting two days to become durable is the cost, and worth noticing.

title: Decision 163 (2026-08-28)
text: A REQUESTED FEATURE IS ASSESSED BEFORE IT IS PLANNED — AND MAY BE ARGUED AGAINST. RESEARCH EXISTING OPEN SOURCE FIRST; DO NOT BUILD WHAT CAN BE ADOPTED. Why: Ian: *“make standing rule when new feature like this is reqquested assess it you may even vouch against it depending on the expected utilization advantage it will give and the effort to make it happen the complexity. research about it always consider open source repo on github there are tons to be used then plan on executing it.”* Three obligations, in order, and the order matters. (1) ASSESS — weigh expected utilisation against effort and complexity, and say the number where one exists rather than the adjective. (2) RESEARCH — the industry pattern *and* what already exists on GitHub, because the default assumption should be that a well-solved problem has been solved. (3) PLAN, only then. Recommending AGAINST is explicitly sanctioned, and therefore expected. §0.3 already says to side with the project over the literal request; this extends it to the existence of the feature itself, not merely its shape. A feature that will be used twice a year and costs a fortnight should be said to be that, once, plainly — and then built anyway if Ian still wants it (§0.4: raise it once, properly, then keep working). The failure this prevents is real and recent: T-141 built a complete upload broker that nothing called for a month, and T-130 then invented a text field because it found no wired upload — effort spent twice, on both sides of

title: Decision 164 (2026-08-29)
text: NO SC/PWD STATUTORY RECORD IS BEING KEPT — NOT IN SOFTWARE, AND NOT ON PAPER. The obligation is unmet today, and rows 131/132 said otherwise. Corrects rows 131 and 132, and answers discovery 24 Open 1 Why: The correction first. Rows 131/132 record *“today the business captures only the ID”*, and T-137 built on it: *“POS already asks for the ID, so the flow exists; it is being widened.”* Verified at source 2026-08-29 across all four reference repos — nothing captures an SC/PWD identity anywhere. POS/src/lib/types.ts:813's Discount carries vatExempt?: boolean and has no ID or name field; the repo's only OSCA-… string is placeholder text in .design-sync/previews/Popover.tsx:16, a component preview. ERP-rebuild, CUSTOMER and Shareat Website have none either. Nobody made a mistake — a practice was minuted as data. Ian's *“we only require the ID”* describes the cashier LOOKING at the card. That leaves no record. Then Ian closed the remaining half, 2026-08-29: *“no they are not kept to avail the discount they just present id and the pos picks the discount from the list of configured discount.”* So there is no paper logbook either. The customer shows a card, the cashier taps a configured discount, and nothing anywhere records the holder's name, ID number or the invoice it applied to. That makes this a live compliance EXPOSURE, not a modernisation project. RR 5-2017 §5.9 and RR 7-2010 both require a separate, per-transaction record and the burden of proof in a BIR audit is on the sell

title: Decision 165 (2026-08-29)
text: ATTENDANCE CREDENTIALS IN v2: FINGERPRINT, FACE AND CARD. NO PIN. AND PROVISIONING A TERMINAL IS ADMIN-ONLY. Why: Ian: *“in v2 only fingerprint face and card will be mode of attendance no pin”*, and separately *“yes admin only”*. Recorded including the misreading, because it nearly went the other way: his first phrasing — *“turn off biometrics by pin”* — was read as *turn off biometrics, use the PIN*; it means turn off the PIN that stands in for biometrics. The two readings put the biometric mirror on opposite sides of the scope line, and only asking settled it. The PIN is made UNREPRESENTABLE rather than switched off — attendance_punches.method drops pin from its CHECK and store_attendance_config drops credential_passcode (migration 0085) — because a kill switch left in the wrong position is landmine #12 in another costume. person_credentials.kind = 'pin' survives: signing in to the app and clocking in are different acts, and only the second is closed. The live data agreed before it was asked: Lipa's production config already reads passcode: false, and across 550 captured August sessions the sources are fingerprint 524, face 10, manual 16 — zero passcode. Zero card, too, so the card rollout is new operational ground rather than a port. provision_clock_terminal is admin-only, tightened from v1's manager-level registerClockTerminalAction: a provisioned terminal is the only principal permitted to read the credential mirror, so whoever may create one may read every enrolled temp

title: Decision 166 (2026-08-29)
text: v1'S ATTENDANCE HAS NEVER PAID ANYBODY — SO v1 IS EVIDENCE OF THE NEED, NOT OF THE RULE. Why: Counted live across all four operating stores while opening Phase 4: 624 attendance sessions in one month, 136 overtime records, 11 absentee records — and payrollRuns, payrollStaffPayouts and payroll all at ZERO, ever. Only 35 of 550 sessions were ever verified (6%). Staff clock in daily, sessions compute, overtime is filed, and not one peso has ever come out the other end. This bounds §1.2b. *“Every feature exists because the business needed it and staff use it daily”* holds for the punch capture and does not hold for the adjudication rule — which Ian names as the reason the module was never adopted. The span-based Tier 1 / Tier 2 start anchor (row 157's rule, 2026-08-20) was therefore replaced rather than preserved: T-157b anchors to the nearest allowed hour, which is how a staffer actually thinks about which shift they are turning up for. The general lesson, and it is the durable half: before treating a v1 module as proven practice, check that anything downstream ever CONSUMED it. Reading the code cannot tell you that; counting the collection can, and it took one command.

title: Decision 167 (2026-08-29)
text: A FLAW SEEN IN PASSING IS LOGGED IN PASSING. THE OBLIGATION DOES NOT WAIT FOR THE TASK THAT OWNS IT. Why: Ian: *“does other agent documents bugs, gaps and flaws they see on v1? if not add that rule.”* The rule already existed and was still not enough — that is the finding. RULES.md row 1, §1.2b, §2.1 and row 80 all say a defect found in a reference repo is logged here and never patched at the source, and DEFECTS-REGISTER.md's own header says *“add a row the moment a defect is found; an unlogged finding is a lost one.”* Every one of those is phrased for an agent already working on that code. Nothing addressed the agent reading v1 for an unrelated reason — tracing a field, checking how a screen behaves — who trips over a flaw on the way to something else. That is where most findings actually come from. Same day, this session found taxTreatment: 'expense' \

title: Decision 168 (2026-08-29)
text: INVENTORY IS PERPETUAL, FROM v2'S FIRST POSTING. THE SIX SHIPPED MODULES ARE RETRO-FITTED; THERE IS NO DATED SPLIT AND NO SECOND POSTING SHAPE. Why: Ian: *“for inventory lets build it right for v2 — everything in v1 plus the inventory being asset and used. That's the model of v1, it just was not realized, so we are building v2 a more robust way. Everything is anchored in inventory: the expense, delivery, usage, wastage etc. So when we test the app we are testing its final deliverable shape and won't need to adjust later.”* The framing is the decision, and it is better than the question I asked. ADR-011 offered retro-fit *or* a dated cutover; Ian's answer is retro-fit and the reason is not accounting neatness but testability — a pilot that exercises an interim shape has not rehearsed anything. The collision this settles: T-133 established on 2026-08-28, by reading the code rather than assuming, that this system is periodic — every expense category maps to a 5xxx COGS account, there is no capitalisation path, and nothing anywhere debited 1310/1330/1340. §10's Phase 3 gate has always required the opposite. Six modules shipped on the periodic shape (T-122 expenses, T-130 AP, T-145 item receipts, T-151 landed cost, T-132 trade orders, T-133 transfers), each correctly following the one before it. The retro-fit costs no data migration and that is not luck — it is ADR-007 and row 106 already working: journal_entries, journal_lines, expenses, sales_days and trade_orders are all class

title: Decision 169 (2026-08-29)
text: A RETURN IS A CREDIT, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS — AND THE GOODS COME BACK INTO INVENTORY AT THE COST THEY LEFT AT. Why: Ian: *“supplier returns must be recognized as store credit for us that we can use for next purchase — that's for external suppliers. Us being the supplier to other customers, return to us must be treated the same I guess: store credit customer may use, or we refund.”* This closes CAPABILITY-GAPS.md's standing “Needs Ian” on supplier returns, and it answers a question nobody had asked — the customer side, which no phase owned at all. v1's supplier return is deliberately stock-and-audit-trail only, with an operator-checked apAlreadyHandled box as a UI nudge; v1 called it *“a documentation gap, not data corruption.”* Under perpetual inventory that compromise stops being available: stock moves and the books do not, which breaks invariant 6 the moment the control account is real. Two directions, and the account each lands in already exists: goods we return to an external supplier credit 1240 Advances to suppliers (party = supplier) when the receipt was invoiced, or 2120 when it was not — because an uninvoiced return simply means they will bill us less, and no credit arises; goods a customer returns to us credit 2140 Customer store credits payable (party = customer), drawn down against their next order, or refunded in cash — their choice, recorded. The inventory half is the part v1 has no concept of at all: returned goods re-enter stock as a new FIFO layer at the cost th

title: Decision 170 (2026-08-31)
text: AN UNVERIFIED SUPPLIER INVOICE MAY CARRY A DRAFT EXPENSE. THE GATE MOVES FROM "AN EXPENSE MAY NOT EXIST" TO "AN EXPENSE MAY NOT POST" (T-196) Why: Ian: *“we will improve that unverified receipt can then be posted against draft expense so cashier does not need verification to start recording. when receipt is verified the expense are posted. when receipt is rejected voided the draft expense is deleted or the posted expense is also voided.”* The rule T-130 built is right; its TIMING was the cost. expenses_check_invoice_open_for_recording() (migration 0043:328) refuses the expense ROW unless its invoice is already verified, and recordExpenseForInvoice requires both create_expense and approve_expense — so a cashier holding only create_expense cannot record an expense at all. Three people, strictly ordered, before a ₱300 purchase reaches the books, and the one person who knows what the money was for is the one who cannot write it down. This is row 126 generalised — *“verification is what posts”*, already the rule for sales days — and row 122 made unconditional: *“Capture is always allowed; VERIFICATION is what is withheld… record the draft with its photo while memory is fresh.”* Row 122 decided exactly this shape for the closed-period case and nothing carried it to the ordinary one. v1 is NOT the precedent here and the spec must not claim it is: v1 writes every expense status: 'posted' immediately (expense.actions.ts:627) and its canTagExpenseToReceipt gate is verified && open — v1

title: Decision 171 (2026-09-05)
text: UI/UX IS A THIRD AUTHORITY, ALONGSIDE §1.2B'S WHAT/HOW SPLIT: v1'S SCREENS ARE FAMILIAR-BUT-UPGRADED, NOT REINVENTED, AND ALL THREE APPS ARE ONE FAMILY. (§1.2c) Why: Ian: *"the ui/ux design of this app must be an upgraded version of v1. i want it to be uniform flexible across screens and respect the workflow of records like v1. all in all i want it to feel familiar but improved one… i want the 3 apps erp, pos and customer to look and feel like they belong to one family… actually in ui POS has cleaner [UI] than erp."* Extends row 6 (*"port the UI layer, rewrite the data layer"*) from a build-order decision into a standing design rule, with three additions row 6 never stated: workflow familiarity is the FLOOR not the ceiling (upgrade the presentation, keep the record workflow recognisable); one uniform, reusable pattern set across screens, the same anti-duplication discipline §4.2 already requires of the data layer; and — new scope — apps/pos/apps/customer (reserved, §8) must share ERP's visual language once built, not diverge as three separate products. Names POS, not ERP-rebuild, as the presentation-quality reference where the two disagree — narrower than §1.2b's WHAT/HOW split, which stays intact: this only says whose *presentation layer* to draw from when duplicating (§1.2). Does not reopen any already-shipped screen.

title: Decision 172 (2026-09-05)
text: DISCOVERY HAS A METHOD, AND IT IS NOW A RULE: STUDY v1 → SYNTHESIZE ITS GOAL IN WRITING → WEIGH WHETHER THE LIVE DATA IS IN GOOD SHAPE → DESIGN v2 AGAINST THAT GOAL, MORE ACCURATE AND MORE EFFICIENT THAN v1 MANAGED. (§1.2d) Why: Ian: *"v1 is a flawed version v2 is the improved version. discovery agent must study v1, synthesize what the v1 feature goal is or it tries to achieve, evaluate the live data if it is in good shape, with the goal of v1 as guide study how v2 can achieve the better more acurate correct improved output in more efffective and efficient way."* Step 3 generalises row 166, which was logged as one module's lesson and never made binding: *"before treating a v1 module as proven practice, check that anything downstream ever CONSUMED it. Reading the code cannot tell you that; counting the collection can, and it took one command."* That sentence has been true of every module since, and nothing obliged the next pass to act on it — so it is now a step, with its consequence stated: bad data downgrades v1 from proven practice to evidence of the NEED only, and the v2 rule is designed from first principles rather than ported. Step 2 is the other addition, and the quieter one. §1.2b already says to ask *what problem was this solving*; it never said to write the answer down. An unwritten goal cannot be improved on — only copied — which is precisely how a flawed implementation survives a rebuild that was meant to correct it. Sharpens §1.2b and replaces nothing: v1 stays au

title: Decision 173 (2026-09-05)
text: §4.2 RULE 7 COVERS EVERY DASHBOARD TILE, NOT ONLY ACCOUNTING STATEMENTS — AND A SEPARATELY-ACCUMULATED COUNTER IS FORBIDDEN EVEN WHEN IT IS CALLED A CACHE. Why: A rule that existed for half the surfaces it should govern. docs/discovery/26 line 325 identified exactly this and could only recommend it: docs/tasks/110 bans maintained summary rows for ledger balances (trial balance, income statement), and nothing extended that ban to operational KPI dashboards — so the discipline protected the trial balance and not *"open disputes"* or *"sales this month"*. v1 supplies both counter-examples, and they fail in two different ways. dashPresets only ever ADDS a receipt to whichever rolling windows currently contain its date, with no mechanism to subtract once a day ages out — observed 3×–11× inflation on "This Month", mitigated by a nightly rebuild cron rather than fixed. dashboardSummary/live self-heals only when a human opens /dashboard and finds it more than 6h stale — SharEat Padre Garcia's was 123.7 hours stale at probe time, because nobody had opened that store's dashboard since 2026-08-30. The second is the more instructive failure, and it generalises past dashboards: a cache whose refresh trigger is a human being has no staleness state at all when nobody looks. T-211 is the first task where this bites, and it lands as ratification rather than redirection — the session building it had already excluded the incremental cache on its own reasoning, before this row existed. Found by

title: Decision 174 (2026-09-05)
text: STORE CREATION IS ITS OWN TASK, NOT HALF OF USER/ROLE MANAGEMENT — AND THE REASON GENERALISES: A PHASE ITEM BUNDLED BY WHERE ITS SCREEN LIVES IS NOT NECESSARILY ONE PIECE OF WORK. Why: Asked of Ian while specifying T-219, because docs/plans/v2-completion-blueprint-2026-09-05.md bundles *"admin/users, admin/stores"* as a single Phase 7 item. Ian: user/role management only; store creation gets its own task. The two halves are different KINDS of work, and only reading the code shows it. User/role management was pure wiring: assignRole/elevateManager and every accessRepo primitive already existed, were tested, and had zero callers — T-219 was their first. Store creation has no backing function at all: packages/db/src/repo/stores.ts holds only cash-custody policy (cashPolicy/setCashPolicy) plus an inbox-relay lookup, and no createStore-shaped function exists anywhere in the repo. Two constraints make it a design pass rather than a form, both found while specifying T-219 and both recorded in that task's *Out of scope*: (1) creating a store means choosing a remittance cadence and unremitted ceiling behind a database check constraint (stores_pooling_requires_ceiling_check), which is a money control, not a text field; (2) CAPABILITY-MATRIX.md §C.2's second half applies in reverse — *"a store created later appears in nobody's scope"* — so createStore must fan person_store_scope rows out to that org's existing admins, or a new branch is invisible to the person who just opened it and the

title: Decision 175 (2026-09-06)
text: A PERSON BELONGS TO EXACTLY ONE ORG. "Ian holds a franchise's org-admin" (row 114) is ONE PERSON ROW PER ORG, not one person holding roles across orgs — and the database now enforces it (T-221, migration 0129, DEF-183) Why: Ian, asked because the migration would have been wrong under the other answer and I was not willing to settle it by inference. person_roles's RLS policy checked the *row's* org_id and never the *person's*, so a cross-org role assignment was accepted by Postgres; its two sibling access tables derive org *through* the person and refuse it. Aligning the three required knowing whether a cross-org role row is a bug or a feature. The registry said feature — *"a person can hold different roles in different orgs, e.g. Ian holding several franchises' admin"* — so it was checked rather than trusted, and it is unreachable: sessions carries no org_id, findLiveByTokenHash selects orgId from persons, no org switcher exists, and authorize() resolves a role only under the person's own org. Such a row therefore has no reader anywhere in the system (filed as DEF-187 — a claim of coverage wearing an *"e.g."* rather than an *"enforced by"*, in the one file whose job is to be believed about tenant isolation). The generalisable half: sibling tables protected by two policy shapes are not interchangeable, and both ended in = app_current_org(). org_id = app_current_org() asks *"is this row LABELLED with my org?"*; the via_person form asks *"does this row's SUBJECT belong to my org

title: Decision 176 (2026-09-06)
text: CREATING A STORE IS TWO HALVES, AND ONLY ONE OF THEM IS THE SYSTEM'S: everything the database can make true by itself is ONE ATOMIC TRANSACTION, and everything that depends on the real world is a DERIVED CHECKLIST, never a stored status — the store row, T-160's default room, and §C.2's admin store-scope fan-out commit together or not at all; whether the branch has staff, a till, a price list or an opening count is *computed on read* from the rows that would exist Why: Ian, 2026-09-06, deciding T-222's shape. The half that is not obvious is the fan-out. A store created without person_store_scope rows for the org's existing admins is invisible to the person who just created it, and presents as a permissions bug rather than a missing step — the same *decided-in-an-ADR-never-written-into-the-function* shape as DEF-180. And the checklist must be derived, not stored: v1's store-provision.actions.ts kicked seeds off fire-and-forget from the client and console.error'd the failure while the UI still said “Store Created” — a success message with nothing executable behind it, which is DEF-185's shape rendered as a toast. v1 built an 11-item readiness registry in response, so it hit this hard enough to pay for a framework. A stored isReady flag would drift the moment someone deletes the price list; a query cannot.

title: Decision 177 (2026-09-06)
text: A RESPONSIVENESS SCORE MEASURES WHAT WAS FIXED, NEVER WHAT WAS ACCEPTED — AND THE CLOCK IT NEEDS IS AN OBSERVATION LOG, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME THING AS STORING A FINDING — the action component counts occurrences that CLEARED (the detector stopped returning the key), acknowledgements are reported beside the score and never inside it, and the unit of scoring is the STORE because a cleared finding has no actor Why: Ian, 2026-09-06, deciding T-214's shape. The naive port re-opens the hole T-135 closed. v1 scored findings a manager marked *resolved*; v2 has no such act. Mapping it onto *acknowledged* pays a manager to ACCEPT risk — acknowledging means the condition still holds and is accepted for 30 days — and the score is then maximised by accepting everything having fixed nothing, which is exactly the gaming row 123's derived model was adopted to prevent. A cleared occurrence needs honesty from nobody. The clock is the hard part and it did not exist: a DetectedFinding is a pure function of current state, carries no timestamp and cannot, and almost no detector can be re-asked *"as of"* a past date — so *when* a condition first appeared was not recoverable from anywhere. finding_occurrences records *"the detector reported this key on this day"* and nothing in the detection path ever reads it, asserted by deleting every row and re-reading the feed rather than promised in a comment. Row 123 stands: what is forbidden is storing a finding's STATE, because state feeds back into detectio

title: Decision 179 (2026-09-07)
text: EVERY v1 FEATURE IS ACCOUNTED FOR IN v2 — CARRIED, FOLDED OR EVOLVED, NEVER SILENTLY DROPPED — AND WHERE v1's DATA SHAPE DRIFTED OVER TIME THE MOST RECENT SHAPE OUTWEIGHS THE OLD Why: Ian, 2026-09-07: *"v2 is an upgrade of v1. all features of v1 might be simplified, corrected, improved but all must be in v2 except faulty and nonsense ones that could be merged/folded to other feature or evolved to new one. same user of v1 and v2, non-techie people so all must feel same and familiar as much as possible. v1 has many inconsistent and unfinished works; its real data might have different shape from day one to most recent because it is being used while being developed. recent data shape must be considered more than old ones. both are tailored to fit the Shareat restaurant system."* Two things this makes explicit that were only implicit before. (1) A completeness guarantee on top of §1.2's four verbs — carry-over is the *default*, deletion the last resort and Ian's alone, with merge/fold/evolve preferred over drop; a v1 feature absent from v2 must be traceable to a verb, never merely un-ported (recorded in §1.2d). (2) A data-recency rule for the discovery method — v1 was developed while in use, so a collection's shape drifts from its earliest documents to its most recent, and v2 is designed against the most recent *consistent* shape; the old shape is migration input at most (recorded in §1.2d step 3). Neither reverses anything already decided: v1 still owns WHAT and never HOW (§1.2b)

title: Decision 180 (2026-09-07)
text: ORDER-WASTAGE "TRACKED VS INSTANT" IS A PER-CHANNEL POLICY, NOT A PER-RECORD CHOICE — the sales channel carries the disposition mode, and the person recording a wastage no longer picks it Why: Ian, 2026-09-07, deciding lane B's Q3. The rejected option is the status quo, which is why it needed deciding: today apps/erp/src/app/wastage/page.tsx lets the recorder choose instant/absorbed per wastage, so a staffer can skip the monitor, the 48h dispute window and the 15-day auto-charge backstop on their own loss — the control is optional to the person it controls. v1 made it a store/channel policy for exactly that reason. It removes a choice staff have today, which is why it is Ian's (a WHAT decision, §0.1) and not the orchestrator's. Built as part of lane B's "sales channels: admin surface + wastage policy" package (with DEF-207): the channel gets a wastage-mode column, the admin surface sets it, and orders.ts reads it instead of the form. Bundled decisions the same day: T-228 pushed to production (Ian runs bootstrap-org himself); DEF-207 → a sales-channel admin surface (not seed-at-creation); DEF-209 → a dedicated RLS-enforcement assessment is scheduled.

title: Decision 181 (2026-09-07)
text: RLS IS ENFORCED AND ALWAYS WAS — the failure was in how we looked for it. THE TENANCY ID NEVER COMES FROM THE CLIENT, and RLS is the second layer behind the repository filter, never the only one and never absent. Why: DEF-209 claimed RLS had zero production callers; the assessment (docs/discovery/29-rls-enforcement-assessment.md) found 310 — the canonical withPrincipal is typed for postgres.js and the app uses Drizzle, so the idiom is copied under another name (DEF-211). Proved live on a lane DB: the connecting role is superuser + BYPASSRLS, and SET LOCAL ROLE shareat_app fully re-arms RLS — zero rows with no principal, own-org only with one, cross-org write refused 42501. 68 of 99 integration files exercise the policies on every CI run. The real defect it uncovered (DEF-210): 5 server actions read orgId out of FormData, on the 3 files that never take a principal — the same shape as DEF-064, on writes. The generalisable half: we had a structural guard for a client-supplied *person* (no-client-supplied-actor.test.ts) and none for a client-supplied *org*, though row 112 calls the org the more consequential of the two. A guard that names one half of an identity is not a guard — T-231 adds the other half. And a method lesson worth more than the finding — it bit TWICE in one afternoon, both times invisibly. A heredoc ate a script's regex escapes so it reported *"0 functions touch an org-scoped table"* and exited 0; a registry parser then silently dropped 5 of 125 entries and publi

title: Decision 182 (2026-09-07)
text: THE CUTOVER WIPES TRANSACTIONAL DATA, NOT STORES AND STORE SETTINGS — the Wastage Monitor survives cutover like every other setting. T-178's carve-out (stores as keep_shell with wastage_monitor_person_id cleared, "re-assigned at cutover") is reversed: stores is keep Why: Ian, 2026-09-07, challenging T-229 slice 3's FOR IAN line that the cutover "wipes this setting on every store". The carve-out was the only column on stores the purge touched, and its justification — *who held that pilot-era responsibility is an assignment to re-decide for production* — grouped the Monitor with customers' reconciliation anchor, which IS cleared because it attests a verification the purge invalidates. The Monitor attests nothing; it is a forward-looking assignment, the same shape as the remittance cadence or the unremitted ceiling, both of which survive. Blanking it would have recreated DEF-206 fleet-wide on cutover morning: every branch in the no-Monitor state, every tracked wastage created ownerless, the 15-day backstop letting each store absorb it — silently, at the one moment nobody is watching. Changing the person for production is an ordinary ten-second edit on /settings/wastage-monitor, not a reason for the cutover to blank the field. Found because slice 3 made the field EDITABLE at all; the cutover policy was a separate question it exposed rather than created

title: Decision 183 (2026-09-07)
text: A RECURRING EXPENSE DRAFTS ITSELF AND NEVER AUTO-PAYS — the job creates a pending supplier invoice and a draft expense, attributed to whoever set up the template, and nothing reaches the ledger until a person attaches the real bill, a SECOND person verifies it, and someone approves. Why: Ian, 6–7 Sep 2026, answering T-216's open question 2; the shape decided by the orchestrator on 2026-09-07 when lane D found the expense path refuses a machine three times (no invoice, no supplier, no human creator). Rejected: a per-org system person for created_by — a persons row that is not a human leaks into every people picker, payroll and attendance, and would have made every recurring invoice self-verifiable. Rejected: relaxing the expense path (nullable created_by, a supplier-less branch) — weakening an audit column for every caller to serve one. Kept: the job acts as the template's creator THROUGH recordInvoice and createExpense with their ordinary authorize gates, so the automation can never do what its author could not (T-216 §8 enforced, not stated); the consequence — the author cannot verify the invoice the job logged in their name — is segregation of duties working, and the screen says so. Idempotency is a database fact: recurring_expense_drafts unique on (template, due date), not the cursor. A due date in a locked period STILL drafts (the lock lives at posting); an overdue template catches up one period per run and the screen says "N periods behind".

title: Decision 184 (2026-09-08)
text: SONNET WHEREVER THE WORK CAN BE DONE BY SONNET — a lane terminal executing an approved spec runs on Sonnet; Opus is for planning, specs and review; the orchestrator names the model in every briefing and lists the terminals to switch on the status board Why: Ian, 2026-09-08, seeing four lanes on Opus while three of them executed approved specs: *"tell agents to use sonnet whenever the work can be done by sonnet… and make that a standing rule."* §3.1a already said it for subagents; this extends it to whole worker sessions. A session cannot switch itself — /model is Ian's keystroke in that terminal — so the rule is applied by the orchestrator naming the model in the briefing and by Ian switching; a lane keeps working through the switch. The escalation bar is unchanged: "it was hard" is not a reason to move a lane up

title: Decision 185 (2026-09-08)
text: FIRST-RUN SETUP IS THE ONE REQUEST PATH THAT OPENS AN OWNER-ROLE TRANSACTION WITHOUT A PRINCIPAL — deliberately, because there is no principal before the first organisation exists Why: Orchestrator, 2026-09-08, recording lane C's finding F1 on T-232's WIP. packages/db/src/rls/principal.ts:38 says an owner-role transaction must never exist inside a request handler; /setup's action must open one, because under shareat_app the zero-organisation read returns zero rows on ANY database and the INSERT is refused by WITH CHECK — the screen can only ever work with the CLI's database posture (T-232 §2.3.2). What replaces the principal: a signed cookie carrying a uid verifyIdToken vouched for, a transaction-scoped advisory lock, and the zero-organisation refusal; the failure direction under a non-bypassing role is a refused INSERT, never a second organisation. Not a precedent. Any other request path wanting owner role is DEF-215's door reopening; this one closes forever after the first organisation, so on every production request after day one the path is dead

title: Decision 186 (2026-09-08)
text: AN ACTOR MAY NOT REMOVE OR DEMOTE A ROLE SENIOR TO THEIR OWN. A PEER MAY. An admin may demote another admin; only a super_admin may demote a super_admin. Ranks are staff 0, manager 1, admin 2, super_admin 3, and the comparison uses effective rank — it reuses holdsSuperAdminAuthority, so an organisation's owner (who holds admin plus the four grants and cannot hold a super_admin row at all) can still remove a super_admin they appointed. The mnemonic "the authority to UNMAKE a role is the authority to MAKE it" is NOT this rule and must not be written down as if it were. Appointing an admin requires super-admin authority (row 116), so built literally the slogan would forbid an admin from demoting a peer admin — which is the "junior only" option Ian explicitly rejected. The sentence is the rule; the slogan contradicts it, and a memorable line that contradicts the rule beneath it is worse than none, because it is the line the next person reaches for Why: Ian's decision, 2026-09-08, asked as DEF-234 and answered "peer removal, and that case is mine". The defect: the super-admin-authority check at packages/auth/src/roles.ts:269 fired only when the new role was admin/super_admin, so appointing an administrator was gated and *unmaking* one was not — removing the person above you was the first move of a promotion. His reason for rejecting "junior only": two admins and no super_admin would mean neither could ever remove the other, turning one rare dependency into a routine one. The conse

title: Decision 187 (2026-09-09)
text: A WORKER SESSION IS CLEARED ONLY AFTER ITS OWN TERMINAL SAYS SO — the orchestrator sends each lane a "SAFE TO CLEAR" notice, in that lane's terminal, when clearing it costs nothing. The notice states *why* it is safe, not merely that it is: nothing in flight · no uncommitted work of that lane's own in the shared tree · no lane state that exists only in the session · its lane database survives and is re-attachable by name · the commit its work landed in. A lane with none of those clear is told plainly that it is not safe yet, and what has to happen first Why: Ian's directive, 2026-09-09, given while clearing four lanes to re-spin them. The problem it solves: from outside a terminal, "idle" and "safe to clear" look identical, and they are not the same thing. On the night this was given, three lanes were genuinely free and the fourth — lane D — held two finished, fully-verified tasks that existed only as uncommitted changes in the shared tree; clearing it would have destroyed nothing, but clearing it *before* the orchestrator committed would have thrown away the only session that could explain them. The lane is the only party that knows its own state, so the lane is where the notice belongs — and putting it in that terminal means Ian reads it where he is standing rather than correlating a chat message to a window. Corollary, same conversation: because lanes are now cleared and re-spun rather than re-adopted, docs/HANDOFF-TODAY.md is written for a cold start — it must brief a ses

title: Decision 188 (2026-09-09)
text: AN ELEVATED MANAGER'S GRANTS ARE REVOKED WHEN THE ORGANISATION GAINS AN ACTIVE ADMINISTRATOR. The elevation is a stand-in for a missing administrator, and it ends when the administrator arrives — it is NOT a permanent promotion, and it is NOT re-derived at check time. The grants stay ordinary person_grants rows, written once at appointment (row 115) and revoked once at admin-arrival: two clear moments, both dated, both attributable, both queryable. The rejected alternative, named so it is not re-proposed: marking the rows *conditional* at grant time and having authorize ignore them once the condition lapses. That reintroduces at the grant layer exactly what row 115 removed at the role layer — a fuzzy predicate (*"does this org have an admin?"*) re-evaluated on every check, on the function everything gates through, leaving a stored row that says active while meaning "active unless something thinks to re-check". Row 115's own reason applies unchanged: auditing would require reconstructing the organisation's admin population as it stood on the day in question. The cost Ian accepted: a manager mid-shift loses those capabilities the instant the revocation commits, with no grace period — if they are part-way through an action gated by one of them, the action they began is no longer one they can finish. That is the price of the grants meaning what person_grants says they mean Why: Ian's decision, 2026-09-09, choosing Option 1 from docs/tasks/244-*.md §6 after lane D (Opus, in plan m

title: Decision 189 (2026-09-09)
text: AN UNMAPPED CONSTRAINT FAILURE IS SANITISED BEFORE IT IS MAPPED — the presentable fallback ships FIRST, and the specific sentences are then written in the order the COUNTER says they are hit. errorMessage() (apps/erp/src/lib/constraint-messages.ts) falls through to raw Postgres driver text whenever no CONSTRAINT_MESSAGES key matches, and it is called from 48 action files — cash requests, loans, AP, AR, money transfers, till, remittance, expenses, budgets, payroll, inventory. Only 21 of the database's 442 CHECK constraints are mapped, so ~420 surface as new row for relation "cash_requests" violates check constraint "..." on the person moving the money. The rule: sanitise the fallback so nothing can ever render driver text again, then instrument it and let measured hit counts decide which constraints earn a hand-written sentence. Reuse T-245's counter, do not build a second one — and reuse it including the part that was hard: T-245's first version wrote its row inside the transaction the refusal aborts, so it would have recorded nothing for ever with nothing red. withOrgPrincipal's independent transaction is the shape that works. A counted hit is a DOUBLE signal, and the second half outranks the first. A constraint only reaches the database when nothing above it refused first, so a hit means *there is no server-side validation on this field*, not merely *this message is ugly*. Proven, not assumed: the one raw failure captured on a real screen got there because createCategoryAct

title: Decision 178 (2026-09-06)
text: PERMITTED UNDERTIME CREDITS THE TIME ACTUALLY WORKED, NEVER THE FULL SHIFT — permission excuses the ABSENCE, it does not pay for the missing time — so a manager who accepts that a short day was authorised approves the PENDING OVERTIME, and does not flip the day to a full one Why: Ian, 2026-09-06, closing T-225 §4. The rejected option is the one v1 effectively implemented, which is why this needed deciding rather than defaulting: v1 paid the full requirement on a day it could not adjudicate, and across the golden corpus it paid more than the person was physically present in 58 of 346 sessions. Adopting that would have been inheriting a defect wearing the costume of a policy. The arithmetic that makes the choice concrete, from payroll/compute.ts — pay is in DAY UNITS (unitsFor() returns 0.5 or 1), the hourly equivalent is dailyRate ÷ requiredHoursPerShift, and overtime pays × overtimeMultiplier. For lipa-0359 (8h worked of a 9h requirement, 1.25 multiplier) against a daily rate D: approving the pending OT pays 0.92 D for 89% of the hours — proportionate; overriding the half day pays 1.00 D for 8 hours — not. And the third row is the one that made T-225 urgent at all: if nobody acts, pending overtime pays NOTHING, so the day settles at 0.50 D for eight hours of work.

title: Decision 190 (2026-09-10)
text: THE CLOCK TERMINAL IS A DOWNLOADED ANDROID APK WITH A FINGERPRINT READER ON AN OTG DONGLE — BIOMETRIC IN AND OUT, THE WAY v1 DOES IT — AND PAIRING IS CONFIRMED BY A MANAGER ON SCREEN, NOT BY THE DEVICE. Nothing in docs/, apps/ or packages/ names an APK build, an OTG dongle, or a fingerprint capture path — the only hits for *apk/fingerprint/biometric/otg* are ADR-002's Google sign-in aside, ADR-003's *“offline is needed for POS selling and the ERP biometric clock only”*, and enrolment code. And it contradicts a stated premise of shipped work: T-203's fingerprint enrolment is labelled on screen as NOT a working capture flow, accepting only pasted template text, justified in DEF-133's disposition with the words *“no capture device exists in this stack”*. The OTG dongle is that capture device. So enrolment-by-paste is a stand-in, not the design, and the real capture + verify path is an unowned gap (CAPABILITY-GAPS.md, added the same

title: Decision 191 (2026-09-10)
text: MIGRATIONS ARE HAND-AUTHORED FROM schema/; npm run db:generate IS RETIRED AND FAILS CLOSED. drizzle-kit generate cannot serve this journal: it stamps when with the wall clock, and the one-day-per-index grid (DEF-091, migration-journal.test.ts) keeps the head months ahead of any clock — 0140 is dated 2026-12-25 — so every generated entry would sort below the head and be silently skipped by the migrator (DEF-039). No drizzle-kit option controls when, and the head advances a day per migration, so the clock never catches up. Every table here also needs what the generator cannot emit (RLS on all 127 tables, 122 policies, expression indexes, EXCLUDEs, 45 triggers), and the snapshot chain broke within the first 20 migrations while the tool still worked and stayed broken for 104 more. The convention lanes were already following is written down with its guards in ADR-012 §5 and packages/db/migrations/README.md; the command itself now says why Why: Ian, 2026-09-10 — *"document this well … so it won't be rediscovered as it was before your work … on bible see where it fits"*, ratifying the dedicated DEF-242 agent's answer to his own question *"repair the generator, or write the convention down?"* The feared failure was MEASURED and did not exist: a snapshot regenerated from today's schema/ was compared object by object against a database built from zero by all 124 migrations — 0 real disagreements across 127 tables, 1,636 columns, 518 FKs, 312 indexes, 356 checks, 4 views (ADR-012 §3). title: Decision 192 (2026-09-10)
text: ROW 189'S CLAUSE *"which is exactly where there is frequently no TS guard either"* IS NARROWED. The unmapped constraint set is GUARDED — the reason those constraints are reachable at all is not an ABSENT guard but a guard that DISAGREES WITH THE CHECK AT THE SUB-CENTAVO BOUNDARY. A correction to one clause of a rationale, NOT a reversal of the ruling. Row 189 stands in full and is unchanged: sanitise the fallback first so nothing can ever render driver text, then instrument it and let measured hit counts decide which constraints earn a hand-written sentence. The sanitised fallback remains the floor precisely because it needs no maintenance. What is corrected is the expected YIELD of the counting programme, and therefore what a hit means when one arrives Why: DEF-275, ratified by Ian 2026-09-10 (raised by lane C during T-255, reported-and-stopped under RULES rule 14 rather than self-amended). title: Decision 193 (2026-09-11)
text: THE FISCAL-PERIOD LOCK GETS AN OVERRIDE FOR admin AND super_admin, AND THIS SUPERSEDES ADR-006's REJECTION OF A GUARDED ESCAPE PATH. A closed period may be posted into by those two roles only, through a transaction-local exemption, with a typed reason and an audit row. What is superseded is narrow and must not be over-read: ADR-006 §7.1 rejected *reopening* — flipping status from closed back to open, which makes the period generally postable again for everyone until someone closes it a second time. Reopening is still NOT built and was not what Ian was asked about. What is now sanctioned is the per-posting exemption: the period stays closed, one authorised entry is let through, and the exemption dies with the transaction Why: Ian's decision, 2026-09-11, answering the orchestrator's escalation with *“new one wins admin and super admin”*. The conflict was found by grepping fiscal_periods across the repo, not by reading either document — neither DEF-284 nor docs/tasks/264-*.md cited ADR-006 at all, so a lane handed only the newer instruction would have built the override without ever learning that the older decision existed. ADR-006 is not wrong and is not withdrawn: its reasoning was that a prior-period adjustment via reverseEntry should be the ONLY correction path, so that no back door exists to lean on. That argument still holds against a *reopen*; it is outweighed for a *narrow, audited, admin-only, self-expiring* exemption, which ADR-006 never evaluated because the option in

title: Decision 194 (2026-09-11)
text: THE CROSS-ORG CALLER LIST OPENS TO FOUR MORE SUBSYSTEMS, AND SIGN-IN GETS ITS OWN NAMED DOOR RATHER THAN SHARING THE SCHEDULER’S. THIS AMENDS ROW 185, WHICH SAID IT WAS “not a precedent”. Row 185 closed the owner-role list at first-run setup and the scheduler and said in terms that it was not a precedent for a sixth caller. One day of arming the tenancy lock found FOUR more subsystems that genuinely cannot scope to one organisation, and the rule as written could not admit any of them: (1) authentication — sign-in, session resolution and sign-out, which read person_credentials and sessions to DISCOVER which org the actor belongs to (DEF-288); (2) runInboxRelayJobs’ store→org resolution (scheduler/index.ts:508); (3) sweepOrphanedFiles (DEF-287), which takes no orgId by design; and (4) the ETL pipeline (DEF-289), whose tables carry FORCE RLS with no policy at all, so no principal can ever satisfy them. Authentication is a CIRCULARITY, not an exception granted for convenience: it exists to find out which organisation you belong to, and RLS wants that organisation declared before it will show you the row that says which organisation you belong to. withOrgPrincipal is not merely wrong on those paths — it is unexpressible. The list stays CLOSED and BUILD-ENFORCED. That part is not relaxed, and it is what caught all four. What changes is that it stops being one undifferentiated list: authentication gets its own separately-named helper, so “may cross organisations because it is a sche

title: Decision 195 (2026-09-12)
text: THE BOOTSTRAP QUESTION — *“has this system been set up at all?”* — JOINS THE CLOSED CROSS-ORG CALLER LIST, AT ALL THREE SITES THAT ASK IT. IT IS A BOOTSTRAP LOOKUP, NOT A FIFTH AUTH LOOKUP, SO IT USES THE DOOR BOOTSTRAP'S *WRITE* ALREADY USED RATHER THAN WIDENING ROW 194'S AUTH DOOR. anyOrganizationExists was left on a bare transaction() by row 194, which admitted four auth lookups and said *“four lookups and nothing more”*. Under a non-bypassing role it reads zero organisations on a populated database, because organizations is RLS-scoped self and no principal is declared Why: Ian, asked directly, ruled *route all three through the bootstrap door*. Sizing it found three call sites, not the one the handoff reserved: sign-in/lib.ts:135 (a stranger is sent to /setup instead of *“ask an administrator”*), setup/lib.ts:28 (the first-run page's own gate, which would render the setup form on a live system), and scripts/bootstrap-org.ts:158 — which contradicted itself, guarding with an unprincipalled read before a write that already used systemTransaction(). The severity was never data: every site is backstopped by the INSERT's own WITH CHECK, so the defect was always *a wrong sentence, never a second organisation*. Say it that way — the first report of row 194's sibling defect said the opposite and the distinction is the whole severity. title: Decision 196 (2026-09-12)
text: THE FISCAL-PERIOD OVERRIDE *DOES* REACH AN ELEVATED MANAGER IN AN ORGANISATION THAT HAS NO ADMINISTRATOR — AND THAT IS INTENDED, NOT A LEAK IN ROW 193. Row 193 grants override_period_lock to admin and super_admin and says *“nobody else”*. But ELEVATED_GRANTS_FOR_ADMINLESS_MANAGER (capabilities.ts:777) is DERIVED as admin-yes / manager-no, so a new admin-only capability enrols itself into the adminless-manager fallback with no edit to any list — assignRole then materialises it as a real person_grants row (roles.ts:106,114). So the two rows, read literally, contradict each other, and the contradiction is invisible: nothing fails, no test goes red beyond a count, and the widening happens at the moment a capability is added rather than at the moment anyone decides anything. Ian ruled the enrolment CORRECT: an organisation with no active administrator has nobody else who could ever authorise a late entry, so excluding the override would not make that org safer — it would make a legitimate correction impossible and push the work to a worse route. The grant is revoked the instant an administrator arrives (row 188), so the widening is self-limiting by construction. Row 193 is therefore READ AS: admin and super_admin in the baseline matrix, plus the adminless-manager fallback that every other admin-only capability already reaches. It is not licence to grant the override to a manager in an org that HAS an administrator, which remains forbidden Why: Ian's decision, 2026-09-12, answering

title: Decision 197 (2026-09-12)
text: sweepOrphanedFiles LEAVES ROW 194'S CLOSED CROSS-ORG CALLER LIST, BY THE ROUTE ROW 194 ITSELF NAMES — IT WAS GIVEN A PRINCIPAL. THE LIST IS NOW THREE SUBSYSTEMS PLUS THE AUTH DOOR, NOT FOUR. Removal from the list did NOT need a fresh ruling from Ian, and the reason is written into row 194: that row says a subsystem can be removed *by being given a principal*, names the orphan sweep as one of the three that could in principle be re-scoped (only authentication is permanent, because its circularity is structural), and re

text: POSITION ACCESS DEFAULTS ARE MATERIALISED person_grants ROWS WITH PROVENANCE 'position' AND A source_ref TO THE DEFAULT THAT WROTE THEM — RECONCILED AT THE FIVE MOMENTS A HUMAN IS PRESENT, NEVER CONSULTED AT CHECK TIME. A position never enters the check path and is never a parameter to authorize() — T-121's warning that *"the moment 'Cashier' becomes a permission, every new job title becomes a permissions change"* stands; a position carries a *default grant set*, which is a different thing. title: Decision 199 (2026-09-12)
text: A RESTRICTED SCREEN IS HIDDEN FROM THE NAV *AND* GATED ON THE SERVER. THIS ADDS DEF-051'S MISSING HALF; IT DOES NOT REPEAL IT. DEF-051 concluded that presentation is not a control, and that conclusion stands unchanged and unqualified: hiding a link remains explicitly insufficient on its own, and a nav filter is never the thing that protects a route. What is added is the second half — every route named in the capability map is refused server-side by requirePageAccess before it renders, and the nav filter and the refusal read from one declaration (apps/erp/src/lib/route-capability.ts) so the two cannot drift. The pairing is the ruling. Either half alone is the defect: a gated route still listed in the nav teaches people to click things that refuse them, and a hidden route with no gate is DEF-051 exactly. Why: Ian's decision, 2026-09-12, given in his own words to the implementing session after he reported the symptom: *"i tried signing in with a staff pin only but i can access many restricted pages and actions for staff"*, and then, asked directly whether to hide the menu or gate the reads, ruling: _"do both hide the menu and gate the reads"_. The reason the pairing is now worth its cost, and it is a fact about the business rather than about the code: this app is used on a shared counter tablet signed in with a store PIN, so the population that can see a screen is not a set of trusted office staff — it is whoever is standing at the till. title: Decision 200 (2026-09-12)
text: A DECISION PUT TO IAN IS PUT IN HIS LANGUAGE, NOT THE REPOSITORY'S. AN ACCURATE EXPLANATION HE CANNOT ACT ON IS A FAILED EXPLANATION. When a session asks Ian to rule on something, the question, the options and the consequences are stated in plain business language — what breaks, who notices, what it costs, what he is choosing between. Identifiers, file paths, capability names and defect numbers may appear as *supporting* detail for the record, never as the substance of the question. This is not a style preference. It is a correctness requirement about the decision, because a ruling made on an explanation he could not read is not informed consent — and this project has already had one: the timer-arming question was answered on a framing that said the jobs would *"find nothing to do"* when in fact they exit failure, and it had to be put to him a second time on the corrected facts. The pattern is what makes it a rule rather than an aside: both times he was being asked to DECIDE, and both times the first explanation was accurate and unusable. The two items were the Caddy request-body limit and the read-gating ruling that became row 199.
