title: Decision 201 (2026-09-13)
text: scripts/provision-terminal.ts JOINS THE CLOSED CROSS-ORG CALLER LIST, BY A NAMED RULING — WHICH IS THE ONLY WAY THAT LIST IS PERMITTED TO GROW. packages/db/src/client.ts states the rule in terms: the system door is *"not a general escape hatch. The list grows only by a NAMED RULING recorded in the bible, never by analogy."* T-304's provisioning script was added to tests/unit/system-transaction-callers.test.ts's closed list with a justification that it is *analogous to bootstrap-org.ts* — which is precisely the reasoning that sentence forbids, so the entry was held and put to Ian. The substance: it has bootstrap's identical circularity and cannot be scoped, and the reason is structural rather than convenient. The script is run once by hand to turn a tablet into a store's terminal; it is given a store, and discovering which organisation that store belongs to is the work. An orgId cannot be an input to a lookup whose output is the org. That is row 194's authentication circularity in a different costume — *"RLS wants that organisation declared before it will show you the row that says which organisation you belong to."* The cost Ian accepted, stated rather than waved at: a person-run script that can read every organisation's stores at once. It is bounded by being manual, --confirm-gated, dry-run by default, and reachable only by someone already holding the droplet, but it is a real widening and the list is now six entries, not five. THE FINDING THAT OUTLIVES THE RULING, AND IT IS

title: Decision 202 (2026-09-13)
text: *Target provisionally superseded by row 275 (pending Ian): if v2 leaves Firebase Auth, the own project shrinks to FCM push.* ERP v2 WILL GET ITS OWN FIREBASE PROJECT, AND UNTIL IT DOES IT BORROWS TWO — IDENTITY FROM v1's ERP, STORAGE FROM v1's POS/CUSTOMER. THE MOVE HAPPENS *AFTER* THE SIGN-IN CUTOVER, NOT BEFORE, AND THE REASON IS THE SEQUENCING RATHER THAN THE COST. Measured 2026-09-13 from the deployed bundle and confirmed independently against Google's Identity Toolkit: v2 authenticates against studio-7300228488-a394e (project number 765051489373, v1's ERP project) and stores files in shareat-hub-v2 (POS + CUSTOMER's). v2 owns neither, and v1 is the system being retired — so the logins of the replacement depend on a project belonging to the thing it replaces. Ian's ruling, asked directly with three options: finish the T-304 cutover on the borrowed project, then move. The trade-off is real in both directions and is recorded so it is not re-argued from one side: moving was *cheapest* at the moment of asking — exactly one Firebase account existed in the whole system — but at that moment email was the only way into production, because PIN sign-in was dead (DEF-333). Changing the identity project has a window in which a wrong setting locks everyone out, with no second door; that is how production sign-in broke on 2026-09-08 (DEF-235). Once PIN sign-in works there are two independent ways in, which is what turns this from nerve-racking into ordinary. The gate is therefore a rul

title: Decision 206 (2026-09-14)
text: PREFER A GUARD TO ! ON A REGEX MATCH; WHERE ! IS USED, A COMMENT NAMES WHAT MAKES IT SAFE. tsconfig.json:12 sets noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true deliberately, so a regex capture group is correctly typed string \ Why: undefined. ! is the one remedy that silently switches that setting off at the point of use — so if it becomes the house reflex, the option stops buying anything while still costing everyone the friction. This is a FRICTION, not a fault, and deliberately not a defect row: nothing is broken, and filing one would be filing a defect against a decision.

title: Decision 207 (2026-09-14)
text: GREP FINDS IDENTIFIERS, NOT PREMISES — AND A PEER’S STATED REASON IS CHECKED SEPARATELY FROM THEIR CONCLUSION. Two halves of one rule. (1) When a change merges or moves two things, the coupling that bites is a premise stated in a comment — true of the old arrangement, false of the new. No literal search finds it, because the code names neither thing. (2) A conclusion can be right while the reason attached to it is wrong, and the reason is what the next person builds on. So before accepting *“the only hardcoded thing is X”*, read each consumer’s stated REASON and ask whether the change falsifies it — and name out loud which two questions used to be the same question and are about to stop being. Why: Three instances on 2026-09-14, and the first would have shipped a silent break of the exact case the task existed to serve. (a) T-316: judgeDraw branches on floatTarget !== null on the stated premise that *“the warn-vs-block split is about whether the ledger can see the whole balance — a takings drawer’s is provisional, a float pot’s is complete”*. True of 1115; false of 1110. An assessment had concluded *“the only hardcoded thing is the CHECK constraint”* after grepping for the account code — correct, and the coupling is semantic, so the migration alone would have flipped every cashier draw from *warn* to *blocked at zero*, refusing the 2pm-buying-ice case Ian had just asked for. (b) T-302/B1: T-304 §Q4 asserted the credential lookup *“LEAVES THE DOOR”*; the shipped code still ope

title: Decision 208 (2026-09-14)
text: AN IDENTIFIER OR FIGURE THE BRIEFING AUTHOR HAS NOT READ IS A GUESS, AND A GUESS WRITTEN INTO A BRIEFING IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A MEASUREMENT. THE ORCHESTRATOR IS THE MOST DANGEROUS PLACE FOR ONE, BECAUSE A LANE STARTS COLD AND HAS NOTHING TO WEIGH IT AGAINST. Seven in a single session, all from the orchestrator, all plausible, all wrong: a guard count taken from a spec while the newer instruction sat in a defect's disposition (*"there is no guard 6"* — there is); a match count copied from a spec margin (*"exactly two, both in one file"* — four, across two); a claim about a terminal's own model (*"never switched off Opus"* — it was on Sonnet, and the lane read its own system prompt to say so); a function name that exists nowhere in the repository (capabilitiesForPerson — it is heldCapabilities); a column that does not exist (primaryPositionId — it is a boolean is_primary on the join row); a *"tree is clean at"* sha the orchestrator itself had already committed past; and a screen sent to a user (*"Staff, then the person, then Credentials"* — the PIN form is on the employment page and Credentials holds cards and fingerprints). Each was generated the same way: from the SHAPE of the thing rather than from the thing. A repository teaches you its naming conventions, and fluency in those conventions produces names that look exactly like the real ones. Plausibility is the failure mode, not carelessness — a wrong name that looked wrong would be caught by the author. THE RULE: read

title: Decision 209 (2026-09-16)
text: THE REPOSITORY STAYS PRIVATE, AND CI COST IS NEVER A REASON TO CHANGE THAT. THE OBJECTION IS NOT SECRETS — IT IS THAT docs/DEFECTS-REGISTER.md IS A PRIORITISED, PLAIN-ENGLISH, FILE-AND-LINE-CITED LIST OF UNFIXED SECURITY HOLES IN A LIVE PRODUCTION SYSTEM. Proposed by Ian as a fix for a GitHub Actions billing block, on a premise that is entirely correct: public repositories get unlimited Actions minutes on standard runners, and it would have unblocked the deploy the same evening. Declined on what it would publish alongside the code. An attacker reading this repository would not need to reverse-engineer anything — the register hands them a to-do list we wrote ourselves, currently naming a permissions check that hides the menu while leaving the data readable, five server actions that take the organisation id from client-supplied form data (a cross-organisation write), a control whose failure mode is a publicly-known secret that does not fail closed, and the finding that SESSION_SECRET is PIN-equivalent key material. WHAT WAS VERIFIED AND IS EXPLICITLY NOT THE REASON, because the usual objection turned out to be clean and saying so keeps this row honest: secrets/ is ignored but for its README, .env variants and *.pem are ignored, and a scan of EVERY commit in the entire history found no secret-shaped file was ever committed — so the risk is not a leaked key, and anyone re-opening this decision should not waste the argument there. title: Decision 210 (2026-09-14)
text: A POSITION, NOT A ROLE, DECIDES WHAT A PERSON MAY DO — THE staff ROLE'S AUTOMATIC BASELINE IS SHRUNK TO NOTHING AND ALL 21 EVERYDAY CAPABILITIES BECOME POSITION GRANTS. Ian's decision, 2026-09-14, shown both options in plain language and answering *"yes A"*. What he was actually reporting: *"still cant turn off record sale submit sales day on dishwasher role and server and panda role they do not have this."* That was never a screen fault. The system has four roles — super_admin, admin, manager, staff — while Cashier, Cook, Server, Dishwasher, Slicer, Inventory Staff and any store-invented position such as Panda are POSITIONS, and every one of them resolves to the single role staff. CAPABILITY_MATRIX granted record_sale to staff, so it reached all seven at once: there is no dishwasher-shaped hole in a role-keyed table. The mechanism needed no invention — authorize()'s axis 3a is already CAPABILITY_MATRIX[capability][role] \ Why: \

title: Decision 211 (2026-09-14)
text: A CAPABILITY REMOVAL SHIPS AS BACKFILL-FIRST, THEN FLIP — NEVER THE FLIP ALONE, AND THE BACKFILL IS THE TASK RATHER THAN A PRECAUTION. Migration 0152 writes one position_capability_defaults row per (active position × store × capability) plus the materialised person_grants for every open employment holding that position, reproducing today's behaviour exactly and changing nothing observable; only then does the matrix flip. The evidence is 0148, which revoked every PIN on 2026-09-14 and cost Ian an afternoon — and an unbackfilled flip is WORSE in the way that matters: 0148 failed at the door before work started, showed *"No sign-in PIN issued yet"* with the fix on screen, left admin email sign-in untouched, and was recoverable from a screen. An unbackfilled capability flip fails mid-shift, per action, says role 'staff' may not 'submit_sales_day', has no second way in, and to recover needs every position at every store configured first. The order is also safe half-deployed, which is why it is stated as an order rather than a transaction: extra grant rows give staff capabilities the old matrix already gave them, so a half-applied release is a no-op rather than a window. AND THE GATE ON THE BACKFILL IS PART OF THE PATTERN, NOT AN ORNAMENT. Ian ruled that an open employment with NO position is a DATA ERROR: 0152 refuses to run and prints exactly who, rather than papering over it. title: Decision 212 (2026-09-16)
text: A MEASUREMENT'S BLIND SPOTS ARE STATED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, OR THE ONE THAT WAS NOT STATED IS THE ONE THAT BITES. T-318's fixture census reported 19 at-risk integration test files and said, carefully and correctly, *"19 is an UPPER bound and is stated as one"* — the intersection could not tell whether a file called a gated function with its staff actor or an admin one. Nobody wrote down that it could also be too LOW. It was: the real number is 20. branch-orders.test.ts carried 30 genuine failures and was invisible to the count. And the blind spot was not where anyone would have looked — the gated-CAPABILITY list was entirely correct. place_branch_order, submitOrder, acceptOrder and addBranchOrderLine were all in it. The STAFF-ACTOR detector was the hole: its pattern accepted 'staff' only when followed by ), i.e. as the last argument, while that file builds its people with mkPerson('Branch cook', 'staff', [br.id]) — 'staff' then a comma, because the helper takes a third parameter. A three-argument fixture helper made an entire file invisible. The second, related hole: direct-call-only reading cannot see a test reaching a gated function through an intermediate, which is why the corrected census closes the gated set transitively over call edges. AND THEN A SWEEP FOUND A 21ST THAT NO CENSUS COULD HAVE FOUND, WHICH IS THE ROW'S REAL POINT. files.test.ts — 16 of 16 red — calls runUpload, which reads authorize(tx, actor, PURPOSE_CAPABILITY[input.purpose], …): the capability is DATA,

title: Decision 213 (2026-09-17)
text: A SCHEMA FILE MAY DELIBERATELY NOT DECLARE A COLUMN — AND WHEN IT DOES NOT, THE NOTE IS THE CONTROL, NOT A COURTESY. T-321 needed a cross-column unique index, which Drizzle can express (generatedAlwaysAs exists in 0.38.4). Declaring it would have put coalesce(card_id, match_token) — the full card id or match token, in clear — into insertCredential's bare .returning() and listLiveForEmployment's bare .select(), invisibly: AttendanceCredentialRow is hand-written and both functions as-cast to it, so the field would be present at runtime and absent from the type. Typecheck would never see it. Settled by running it, not arguing: .toSQL() shows Drizzle emits an EXPLICIT column list built from the table and never select */returning * — so a column absent from the Drizzle table can never appear in either query, by construction rather than by caller discipline. This is a deliberate departure from ADR-012 §5 step 3 (*"every rule Drizzle CAN express lives in the builder AND in the SQL"*), recorded here rather than left as undocumented divergence. The house already had the pattern — employment.ts:218 carries a bare // NOTE: for the lower(staff_code) expression index. Why: Found by the auditor lane BEFORE the schema file was written, from reading the spec — the cheapest possible moment. The NOTE must carry the WHY and not just the what: T-321's first draft explained the index thoroughly and deleted two rationales that existed nowhere else — *"an ambiguous credential check that picks the f

title: Decision 214 (2026-09-17)
text: A REWRITE IS A DELETION TOO, AND THE DELETION CHECK MUST BE EXHAUSTIVE OVER THE REMOVED SIDE. Reviewing a diff for what it ADDS audits half of it. Every replaced comment, renamed function and reworded user-facing string must also be asked: what did this stop saying, and does that survive anywhere else? And finding one thing is not finishing — the sharpened half, which is the half that was learned the hard way. Why: Coined by the auditor lane (webapps-f7) after T-321's rewrite of resolveScan's doc comment deleted a TRUE sentence (T-185 / landmine #22, the guardrail against a terminal asserting an employment) along with the false claim it was sent to fix. Then the rule half-worked on its author's orchestrator and that is why it is a bible row rather than a note: the orchestrator applied it to the schema comment, found the *"wrong person gets paid"* rationale, restored it — and stopped looking. A second rationale in the same removed block, explaining why the index is PARTIAL (badge reissue), went past everyone until the auditor enumerated all eight removals. Its only other copy was inside an applied migration, which RULES §1 rule 9 forbids editing and nobody opens while editing a schema. The backstop that would have caught it was a test, not a reader — spec test 5 — so it was caught but never explained.

title: Decision 215 (2026-09-17)
text: A SLICE HANDED FOR REVIEW IS FROZEN: NO LANE EDITS ANY FILE IN IT UNTIL THE ORCHESTRATOR RELEASES IT. Anything urgent goes to the orchestrator as a message, and the orchestrator decides whether to unfreeze. A held file belongs to its owner for RUNNING as well as editing — running another lane's test produces a number that looks like evidence under the wrong session's name. Why: Three times in one day the working tree moved under an active review: a tester's file gained a test mid-read, the orchestrator had the builder add an export to a file already handed out (and never told the reviewer, voiding a review it then quoted as clean), and a manifest test was rewritten between two reads minutes apart. The third nearly produced a false finding — the auditor read the OLD assertion and was composing *"the ruling is declared but not implemented"*, a serious and entirely wrong claim, and caught itself only because it habitually RUNS things rather than reasoning about them. The rule existed before the third incident and failed anyway, because it had been written as an instruction to the ORCHESTRATOR and never told to the lanes — who were editing files they had no way of knowing were under review, doing exactly what they had been asked, at the moment they had been asked. A rule only one party knows is not a rule.

title: Decision 216 (2026-09-19)
text: THE SALES DAY RECOGNISES THE REVENUE; THE REMITTANCE ONLY ANSWERS *WHERE THE MONEY IS*. A SHORTAGE KEEPS THE DAY FROM BEING FULLY REMITTED RATHER THAN BEING DISPOSED OF, AND AN OVERAGE IS OTHER INCOME. Ian's decision, 2026-09-19, given in his own words when asked what resolving a POSITIVE remittance variance should mean (DEF-380): *"mirror what v1 workflow does sales report submited, verified. once verified it is recognized as sales, remittance is just money movement where is the money. shortage will keep sales day from being closed=fully remitted so manager can always go back and charge or mark as remit when staff pays shortage by cash. overage will be considered other income."* FOUR RULINGS, AND TWO OF THEM CONFIRM THE BUILD RATHER THAN CHANGE IT. (1) Verification is recognition. Already exactly what v2 does — packages/domain/src/sales-days/verify.ts opens *"Verification IS the posting. That is the whole design"*, and an unverified day carries no journal entry, so it contributes revenue to no reader. This ruling makes that an authority rather than an implementation choice. (2) A remittance is money movement, not revenue. Also already true: createRemittance posts a createMoneyTransfer and reads journal_lines to derive what a day owes; it recognises nothing. The consequence is the part that was NOT understood: because the sales day already recognised the revenue, a remittance variance can never be a revenue adjustment — it is only ever a statement about cash location or cash

title: Decision 217 (2026-09-20)
text: THE BUSINESS COLLECTS THE STATUTORY CONTRIBUTIONS AND REMITS THEM TO THE AGENCIES ITSELF, SO T-190 AND T-193 ARE BOTH IN JANUARY SCOPE — INCLUDING THE EMPLOYER SHARE v1 LEFT OUT. Ian, 2026-09-20: *"the business collects it and remit to the agencies"*, confirming that each pay run deducts the employee share, adds the employer share, and the business remits the total to SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG and BIR. This settles what §16.7 defect #1 recorded as out of scope in v1: the EMPLOYER share (6110–6130) is real expense the business bears and must post, and T-193's remittance settles 2210–2240 rather than leaving them to accumulate. And the data gate on T-190 now has an OWNER AND A DATE: it was blocked by *"0 of 126 staff have an SSS number"*, and Ian ruled *"HR collects it by end of october"* — the SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG and TIN numbers for all 126 staff, by end of October 2026. Suggested start trigger, per T-190's own note: the task may begin when the first employment carries a real SSS number, rather than waiting for all 126. Why: Payroll that deducts but never remits leaves a growing liability nobody settles, and an employer share that never posts understates the cost of every employee. Both were v1 gaps rather than v1 practice, so §1.3's *practice wins* does not apply — there is no practice to preserve. The date matters more than the scope: T-190 was blocked on data no task could produce, and a task blocked on someone else's collection work is not scheduled, it is only liste

title: Decision 218 (2026-09-20)
text: THE SENIOR-CITIZEN AND PWD DISCOUNT IDENTITY IS CAPTURED AT THE POINT OF SALE, IN THE v2 POS APP — NOT IN THE ERP. T-137's ERP HALF THEREFORE WAITS ON THE POS BUILD. Ian, 2026-09-20: *"capture at POS when POS will be made"*. The statutory register T-137 produces is fed from POS, so the ERP side has no input until apps/pos exists — and apps/pos is reserved, not built. Until then NOTHING captures the name and ID anywhere, so the blueprint §7 item 3 exposure stays OPEN; it is now *scheduled behind the POS build* rather than sitting unowned in the ERP backlog. Only half of §7 item 3 was ruled. BIR 1601-E expanded withholding on supplier payments — the other half — is still unruled, and is not to be treated as settled by this row. Why: The discount is granted at the till, so the identity exists at the till; asking the ERP to capture it later means asking a bookkeeper to reconstruct who was served. Recording it where it happens is the only version that can be accurate, and it is where the statutory register's own source data has to come from.

title: Decision 219 (2026-09-20)
text: SIGN-IN THROTTLING IS APPROVED TO BUILD NOW — DEF-063's DEFERRAL IS LIFTED, AND IT IS T-331. Ian, 2026-09-20: *"3 yes on pin trotling"*. DEF-063: sign-in has no rate limiting at all, and a 6-digit PIN is a million guesses. The point of building it NOW is that no terminal is in front of a cashier yet — a throttle added before the first device ships is a design; added after, it is an incident. The remedy the register already names: per-store AND per-device attempt throttling with a lockout, and the attempt log feeds the OIL findings engine (T-135) as a finding — *"repeated failed sign-ins at one terminal"* — not as a log line nobody reads. T-331 is allocated to this; the spec is still to be written, and it is a lane-sized slice, not a sweep. Why: An unthrottled 6-digit PIN is not a weak control, it is the absence of one, and the attendance and cash paths both sit behind it. And a failed-sign-in log that only exists in a log file is the same defect one layer out: the evidence of an attack would be present and unread, which is why it goes to the findings engine rather than to stdout.

title: Decision 220 (2026-09-20)
text: SUPPLIERS ARE PAID IN FULL, TAXES AND CHARGES INCLUDED — SO BIR 1601-E EXPANDED WITHHOLDING IS OUT OF SCOPE FOR v2. Ian, 2026-09-20: *"we pay the full amout to supplier including all tax and charges"*. No withholding line on a supplier payment, no BIR 2307 issued to a supplier, no 1601-E remittance flow. This closes the SECOND half of blueprint §7 item 3 — the half row 218 explicitly left open — as a business decision rather than as a build, and the two halves are now settled by opposite answers: SC/PWD identity IS captured (at POS, row 218), EWT is NOT withheld. THE RULING IS RECORDED WITH THE UNDERSTANDING IT WAS MADE ON, because the caution was given and not re-argued: if the business is legally a withholding agent for any payment class — rent to a landlord is the usual one — then paying in full does not discharge the obligation, and the exposure is the business's rather than the system's. That is a question for the accountant, not for v2, and this row says so rather than implying the legal question was answered by the scoping one. Why: Withholding is an obligation the business either has or does not have; a system that withholds where the business does not is as wrong as one that fails to withhold where it must. Ian is the one who knows which supplier relationships exist, so scoping follows his answer. The value of the row is the distinction it preserves: "v2 does not build it" and "the obligation does not exist" are different claims, and only the first was decided here.

title: Decision 221 (2026-09-20)
text: T-187 (SERVICE-CHARGE DISTRIBUTION, CLEARING 2160) IS BUILT NOW AND THE SERVICE CHARGE STAYS SWITCHED OFF — THE CLEARING MECHANISM EXISTS BEFORE ANYONE CAN ENABLE THE THING THAT NEEDS IT. Ian, 2026-09-20: *"service charge build but turn off"*. This defuses the DEF-082 landmine by SEQUENCING rather than by a warning: every sales day carrying a service charge credits 2160, and nothing clears it — so the account grows and no distribution ever happens. The blueprint's operational tripwire was a sentence (*"do not enable service charge in POS before this exists"*), and a sentence is only as good as the person who reads it at the wrong moment. Build-then-enable makes the tripwire structural: by the time the switch can be flipped, the mechanism it depends on is already shipped and tested. T-187 moves from "unbuilt on purpose until service charge is switched on" to a SCHEDULABLE task — and the switch itself stays off pending a SEPARATE ruling, which is the half that must not be quietly folded into this one. Not urgent for the November gate precisely because the switch stays off; it is sequenced after T-330 and the DEF-395 re-derivation. Why: A guard that must be built *before* it is needed is the only kind that is ever built in time; one scheduled for the day it becomes necessary is scheduled for the day after. And the shape is one this project has been bitten by repeatedly: a correct instruction (*"do not enable X first"*) sitting in a document, protecting a liability account nobody

title: Decision 222 (2026-09-20)
text: THE SERVICE CHARGE IS TURNED ON SO IT CAN BE TESTED — AND THE MEASUREMENT THAT ANSWERS IT IS THAT THERE IS NOTHING TO TURN ON. Ian, 2026-09-20: *"service charge turn on so we can test"*. Measured before recording, not inferred: grep for featureFlag/serviceChargeEnabled across packages/ and apps/ returns nothing; sales_days.service_charge is an ordinary numeric column defaulting to '0' (packages/db/schema/sales-days.ts), createSalesDay takes serviceCharge?: string and defaults it to '0', and /sales-days/new already renders a Money field labelled *"Service charge (→ 2160 float, held for staff)"*. So in THIS app the service charge has been enterable all along — type an amount on a sales day and it credits 2160 today. The switch DEF-082 warns about is a POS setting, and apps/pos is reserved and unbuilt (row 218). Therefore this ruling requires no code change to be satisfied, and no feature flag is to be invented to satisfy it — building a switch so it can be turned on would be scope invented out of a sentence. What the ruling DOES decide is the half row 221 left open: the enable decision is GRANTED for testing, and T-187 is therefore pulled forward to the next lane after T-330 — ahead of the DEF-395 re-derivation, which row 221 had sequenced it behind — because a service charge that can be entered and never cleared is DEF-082 running, not waiting. Why: Ian asked to turn a thing on in order to test it; the honest answer is that the entry side needs no permission it does not alread

title: Decision 223 (2026-09-20)
text: T-187 RECORDS THE PAYOUT; IT DOES NOT COMPUTE IT. THE SPLIT, WHO IS ELIGIBLE, AND THE ODD CENTAVO ARE ALL OUT OF THE ERP'S SCOPE BY IAN'S EXPLICIT DECISION. Ian, 2026-09-20, verbatim: *"the business will collect it and dispense it every payday. thats all erp should record. as to split erp wont know that, who counts erp does not have to know. odd centavo erp not know too, per store , pay only whats available never negative ----- ALL erp does not have to know will be processed manually and documented manually too."* And, in the same breath: *"simplify its build."* RELAYED via webapps-17, not typed in the orchestrator's terminal — recorded with his words verbatim, put back to him for confirmation, and CONFIRMED by him the same evening (*“1 yes”*), with no corrections. The standing rule held and cost one round trip: a relay is information, and it became authority only once he said so. THIS ANSWERS THREE QUESTIONS BY DISSOLVING THEM, WHICH IS NOT WHAT WAS ASKED AND IS BETTER THAN WHAT WAS ASKED. Q1 (split formula), Q2 (rank-and-file eligibility) and Q3 (rounding) were put to him as design choices; he removed them from the system instead. Consequences that follow and must not be re-litigated: NO eligibility field and therefore NO schema change; NO per-employee computation; NO rounding rule in code. The business computes and documents all three by hand, outside the ERP. Q4 — 2160 IS PER STORE. This makes serviceChargeFloatAgeing WRONG as built: it groups by je.entry_date only, with

title: Decision 227 (2026-09-24)
text: MESSAGES ARE SHORT. Every report, to Ian or between sessions, carries only what its reader must act on (§3.5a). Ian: *"messages eats most of my token… only bring to my attention things that really needs me and dont over explain everything happening… goal is to lower token usage by messages."* Why: Orchestrated sessions were spending most of their token budget on cross-session and user-facing narration that nobody acted on.

title: Decision 226 (2026-09-20)
text: IAN ORDERED A STORE-SETTINGS SCREEN FOR DEFINING PAYDAYS, AND THE MEASUREMENT WAS THAT IT ALREADY EXISTS — SO T-332 IS THE CHECK, NOT THE SCREEN. Ian, 2026-09-20: *"create a doc on store settings where admin define the date of paydays."* Measured before recording, by a read-only census (webapps-17): store_attendance_config already holds payrollPeriodType, semiMonthlyCutoffDay, payoutMode, payoutLagDays and payoutDays, effective-dated, one live row per store; /settings/attendance already edits them under manage_store_settings, admin and manager; and packages/domain/src/payroll/periods.ts already derives periods and payout dates from them. All shipped under T-189c/T-189d. The instruction is therefore satisfied on its face — the same shape as row 222, where the order was to turn the service charge on and the measurement was that there was nothing to turn on. WHAT IS GENUINELY MISSING, AND IT IS SMALLER AND MORE USEFUL: nothing CHECKS the recorded cadence against RA 11360, and DEF-249 covers it — a freshly bootstrapped store has no config row at all, so the screen renders empty and the policy is recorded nowhere. Specced as T-332. Recorded as a ruling SATISFIED plus a defect FOUND, not as an instruction declined — building the screen again would have been days spent re-creating shipped work, and RULES §4 makes saying so plainly the obligation rather than the liberty. Why: The order was to create something that already existed. Re-creating it would have cost days and produced a se

title: Decision 225 (2026-09-20)
text: THE BUSINESS PAYS EVERY 15 DAYS, WHICH CLOSES ROW 223'S RA 11360 CAUTION — AND RUNNING THE REPO'S OWN CODE FOUND THE EXPOSURE IS ZERO SLACK, NOT OVERSHOOT. Ian, 2026-09-20, typed directly into the orchestrator terminal rather than relayed: *"our set up follows payday every 15 days."* Fifteen days is inside the statute's sixteen-day ceiling, so the *"verify every store's configured cadence before calling T-187 done"* instruction in row 223, in docs/tasks/187-*.md §2 and in the handoff is DISCHARGED BY THE RULING — Ian has stated the business's actual cadence rather than us inferring it from T-189's per-store cutoffs. THEN IT WAS MEASURED, AND THE HYPOTHESIS WAS HALF WRONG IN THE MORE USEFUL DIRECTION. Row 223 feared *"a month with a 31st can stretch a semi-monthly gap to 16-17 days."* webapps-17 ran the UNMODIFIED derivePeriods and payoutDateFor across 2026 and leap-year 2028 on the schema defaults: the maximum gap is exactly 16 days and never 17 — but it hits 16 in seven months of every year, every 31-day month, 15th to 31st. monthly breaches every month by 12 to 15 days; weekly never exceeds 7. SO THE NUMBERS SUPERFICIALLY SUPPORT "THE CONFIG ALREADY GUARANTEES COMPLIANCE", AND THAT IS THE WRONG CONCLUSION. Sitting exactly ON the ceiling seven times a year means any one-day slip — a weekend, a holiday, payroll run late, payoutLagDays bumped off 0 — breaks the statute. Work out the DIRECTION of an error before its SEVERITY (row 224's lesson, holding again): a gap measured too

title: Decision 224 (2026-09-20)
text: AN UNTICKED ALLOCATION BOX COUNTS AS EMPTY, SO AUTO-ALLOCATE REFILLS IT — IAN DECLINED THE CHANGE AND THE CURRENT BEHAVIOUR IS THE RULED ONE. Ian, 2026-09-20, asked directly whether unticking should mean *“leave this alone”*: *“2 no change needed.”* Context, because the question only exists because of how T-330 was built: ruling 2 (row 211 / AMENDMENT 7) is *“fill only the EMPTY boxes, never overwriting a typed amount”*. A cleared or unticked box holds no typed amount, so it is EMPTY and the ruling is not engaged — the orchestrator ruled it that way during T-330's audit round 2, and Ian has now confirmed the outcome. The known consequence, accepted rather than overlooked: unticking is the natural *“not this one”* gesture, and pressing Auto-allocate afterwards undoes it. The operator must clear the box AND not press the button again, or edit the figure after allocating. Why: The alternative — *“cleared means deliberately excluded”* — is a perfectly reasonable rule, and it is a NEW one. It was refused entry BY INFERENCE inside a bug fix and put to Ian as a question instead, which is the whole point: this task recorded three separate occasions on which a rule nobody made arrived inside a tidy-up, a fix or an amendment, and each cost a spec amendment. A fourth was available and was not taken. And the safe half is what made deferring cheap: the behaviour is VISIBLE — the box refills on screen, the figure is editable, and nothing posts differently without the operator seeing it. A

title: Decision 205 (2026-09-14)
text: PRODUCTION PUBLISHES THE COMMIT IT IS RUNNING, AT /api/health, UNAUTHENTICATED — AND THE DISCLOSURE IS AN ACCEPTED COST, NOT AN OVERSIGHT. /api/health gains revision: { sha, builtAt } on every response including both 503s. Ian's decision, 2026-09-14, taken after being told in plain language that the endpoint is unauthenticated and that this tells a stranger the age of the running build; the alternative put to him was a private file on the box, read over the deploy SSH path, which costs an extra credential and extra wiring. What a stranger gains is the AGE of the build, and therefore whether a publicly-disclosed dependency vulnerability is plausibly still present. What they do not gain: the repository is private, so a sha is not a lookup key for anyone outside it, and nothing about configuration, routing or data is revealed. This must NOT later be "fixed" by redacting the field in production. route.ts:14-17 already withholds error detail in production, deliberately; the revision field does not use that path, and adding it would silently break the lag guard (T-308 slice B), which reads the field over loopback and cannot distinguish redaction from a stale build. The sha is published in full (40 chars) with builtAt beside it, not abbreviated — abbreviation buys no privacy (a prefix is equally resolvable to anyone with repo access and equally useless without) while costing the guard precision by forcing prefix comparison. builtAt earns its place because a sha answers WHICH commit

title: Decision 204 (2026-09-14)
text: A REMEDY IS AS PERISHABLE AS A DIAGNOSIS. ANY COMMENT OR REGISTER ROW THAT NAMES A SPECIFIC TOKEN — AN IDENTIFIER, A LINE NUMBER, A SECRET, A FILE — AND ASSERTS A PRESENT-TENSE FACT ABOUT IT WILL GO STALE WITHOUT ANYBODY EDITING IT. RECORD THE RULING; NEVER A CONDITIONAL INSTRUCTION. Six instances in one morning, 2026-09-14, and not one was caught by anyone re-reading anything on purpose. (1) DEF-338 — a test comment said *"whoever fixes that root cause should come back and delete this timeout override"*; the root cause had been fixed eleven lines below it, so the instruction was live and following it would have deleted a safeguard another row forbids removing. (2, 3, 4) DEF-338's and DEF-334's own rows cited :541-546 for a block at 542-547, :549-556 for one ending at 555, and :538 for a line that had stopped saying what it claimed. (5) The repair moved a fifth: the replacement comment was six lines longer, pushing the override it protects from :627 to :633 — *the fix for the stale-citation defect created a stale citation in the row describing it, within the hour.* (6) DEF-346 — deploy.yml's required-secrets comment names eleven secrets and the workflow reads seven. THE RULES THAT FOLLOW. (a) Prefer a NAME to a POSITION. An identifier survives every edit above it; a line number does not. Cite scratchName, not :557. (b) Phrase it as a ruling, not as *"whoever does X should then do Y"* — that is a booby trap with a timer, because X eventually happens and nothing links the two.

title: Decision 203 (2026-09-13)
text: A RELEASE MAY SHIP WITH A §9 DEFINITION-OF-DONE GATE UNMET — BUT ONLY ON IAN'S EXPLICIT AUTHORISATION, GIVEN AFTER BEING TOLD IN PLAIN LANGUAGE EXACTLY WHICH GATE DID NOT RUN AND WHAT THAT LEAVES UNPROVEN. THE AUTHORISATION IS THE EXCEPTION; THE SILENCE IS THE DEFECT. §9 requires integration tests against real Postgres, and §13/DEF-245 make CI the only real integration gate because the full suite OOMs locally. On 2026-09-13 the sign-in rewrite reached production with that gate never having run anywhere — OOM-killed twice locally, and CI itself disabled_manually for nine hours (DEF-336), so git push created zero runs. Ian was asked twice. The first framing offered a normal push; when the disabled workflow was discovered the question was put again on the corrected facts — *"nothing anywhere has fully tested the change we are about to put on your front door"* — and he chose to deploy. It was the second question that mattered, and it existed only because the premise of the first had collapsed. What this row permits is narrow: shipping with a named gate unmet, when the person carrying the business risk has been told which one and what it protects. What it does NOT permit, and these are the failure modes it exists to forbid: (1) reporting such a release as "green" — §9 is unchanged and a task reported complete with an unmet gate is still a defect; the wrap-up must name the gate that did not run, which is why this day's handoff says *quote the gates table, never the word "green"*; (

title: Decision 228 (2026-09-27)
text: PUSH ONLY AT WRAP-UP. Slices are committed locally as they land; the tree is pushed ONCE, at wrap-up, unless Ian says otherwise. Ian, 2026-09-27, standing. Why: Each push triggers CI and a status round for nobody's benefit mid-day; wrap-up already runs the real gates and pushes everything, so one push per day loses nothing.

title: Decision 229 (2026-09-28)
text: EVERY REFUSAL A PERSON CAN SEE NAMES THINGS IN WORDS — NEVER AN ID, A CODE OR A KEY. A refusal says *which* record, person, store or field in the words the reader uses (a name, a date, a label), never a UUID, enum value or column name. Ian's ruling behind T-343 (docs/tasks/343-def-417-human-readable-refusals.md, DEF-417). Why: DEF-417: the org ADMIN was refused with a raw person id and org id — accurate and useless. A refusal the reader cannot act on is a failed refusal (row 200's rule, applied to the product).

title: Decision 230 (2026-09-28)
text: A POST-COMMIT /code-review OF A WORKTREE RUNS IN A SESSION OPENED *AT* THAT WORKTREE. Passing the worktree path as an argument still reviews the MAIN tree. Auditor finding, 2026-09-28 (T-343 S5.5w Amendment A1 came from such a review of 7896e2a, run in the worktree). Why: A review pointed at the wrong tree returns a clean-looking result for code it never read — green, and about nothing.

title: Decision 231 (2026-09-28)
text: A REFUSAL MAY NAME ONLY RECORDS THE ACTOR MAY SEE AT *THIS* STORE. Naming a record in words (row 229) must never become a way to read another store's data: every lookup made to name something is scoped by the same store (and org) as the act being refused. DEF-453 (docs/DEFECTS-REGISTER.md): an AP payment refusal named another STORE's expense because the name lookup filtered by org only. Why: Row 229 turns every refusal into a read path; without this rule a forged id in a form leaks another store's particulars through the error text.

title: Decision 232 (2026-09-28)
text: "HOLD IN THEIR OWN RIGHT" KEEPS THE GRANT AT THAT STORE (Ian, DEF-456) — AND A HAND GRANT OF A CAPABILITY ALREADY HELD AUTOMATICALLY *CLOSES AND REPLACES* THE AUTOMATIC ROW, NEVER RE-LABELS IT. Design: T-349 (docs/tasks/349-def-456-store-scoped-hold-own-right.md) — the hand grant coexists with the position-sourced one at the same store rather than upgrading it, which supersedes the mechanism of T-291 decision 5 (the in-place provenance upgrade). Ian, Q1 YES (2026-09-27): rows DEF-456 already widened to every store are re-scoped by migration 0166 (T-349 §3.5, S3). Ian, Q2 "close and replace" (2026-09-28): the automatic row is revoked ("Replaced by a hand grant of the same capability.") and a new hand-grant row names the clicking actor and the time (T-349 §4c, §9). Q2 supersedes row 188's in-place re-label of an elevated grant; row 188's revoke-on-admin-arrival rule stands. Why: The old button silently widened a store-scoped capability to every store, which nobody chose; and a re-label kept the automatic source's name on a row a person granted by hand, so the audit trail lied about who decided. A revoke plus a new row keeps both who and when.

title: Decision 233 (2026-09-28)
text: A TEST ASSERTS THE TARGET, NEVER TODAY'S BEHAVIOUR. A red test states the sentence or value the spec requires; it is never written to match what the code currently produces and then "fixed" later. (Applied throughout T-343 and T-349: *"Every leg asserts the TARGET. Record the raw red."*) Why: A test that pins current behaviour goes green on the bug and red on the fix — it certifies the defect.

title: Decision 234 (2026-09-28)
text: MONEY, QUANTITY AND NUMBER INPUTS ARE TEXT INPUTS WITH inputMode, NEVER type="number"; THE SERVER REFUSES UNPARSEABLE TEXT BY NAME; AND CHECKS ARE ON THE VALUE, NEVER ON THE DIGIT RUN. Chrome turns 1,5 into 15 in a number box and silently drops what it cannot parse. So: the box accepts what was typed; the server parses it, and on failure refuses naming the field (row 229); .5, 005 and 8. are accepted; any ceiling is stated in the refusal. T-343 S5.5s–S5.5w (docs/tasks/343-def-417-human-readable-refusals.md, DEF-470). Why: Measured in Chrome 152: the browser changes or drops input before the server ever sees it, so no server rule can recover the person's intent. Digit-run regexes refused valid values people actually type.

title: Decision 235 (2026-09-28)
text: BLANK MEANS "NOT DECIDED", NOT ZERO. Ian, 2026-09-28: a blank attendance minutes box (overtime etc.) leaves the decision open, never "approve 0 minutes" (DEF-471). Blank whole-number attendance settings are refused by name — except auto clock-out, where blank = never. Blank channel-settlement gross and net are refused. T-343 S5.5t–S5.5w. Why: Turning '' into 0 recorded a real decision nobody made (DEF-471). A setting has no "undecided" state, so blank is refused rather than guessed — except where blank already has a stated meaning.

title: Decision 236 (2026-09-28)
text: A CHANNEL'S PAYOUT ACCOUNT IS SET AND CHANGED BY ADMIN ONLY — NEW STORE-SCOPED CAPABILITY set_channel_payout. Ian, 2026-09-28. Managers see the account but cannot set or change it. T-350 (docs/tasks/350-def-477-change-channel-payout-account.md), DEF-477; matrix row in docs/decisions/CAPABILITY-MATRIX.md. text: A REMITTANCE SHORTAGE IS ALWAYS CHARGED TO THE PERSON RESPONSIBLE — NEVER WRITTEN OFF; AN OVERAGE BECOMES INCOME ONLY WHEN A MANAGER CONFIRMS IT (T-366 Q1, Q3, Q2).
